title: The Animal Kingdom in One Level
objective: After this level you can explain what makes an animal an animal and name the main groups.
summary: An animal has many cells without walls, eats other living things and usually moves at some stage. Sponges qualify. The kingdom: five familiar groups and a vast crowd without backbones.

cards.headline: Sponges were long mistaken for plants.
cards.body: They have no muscles, and a grown sponge stays stuck to one spot for life. Only after someone noticed their small movements, in 1765, did people slowly accept sponges as animals. So what does it actually take to be an animal?

cards.headline: The animal checklist
cards.body: Biologists use a short checklist. An animal is built from many cells, and unlike plants and fungi, those cells have no cell walls. It can't make its own food, so it eats other living or dead things. And most animals can move, at least at some stage of life. Fur, legs and a face are all optional. Eating someone else's lunch is not.

mascot.line: Swim once, then sit still forever. Honestly, a very relaxing life plan.

cards.fact: A sponge does all its traveling as a baby.
cards.context: Sponge larvae can swim. Then they settle, attach and stay put for good. The adult feeds by pulling water through its porous body, where tiny hairlike flagella stir up currents that bring in bacteria to eat. Many cells, no cell walls, eats other living things, moved at one stage of life: a sponge ticks every box on the checklist.

items.label: The crowd you overlook
points: Worms, jellyfish, sea stars and sponges

title: How Many Species?
objective: After this level you can explain how many animal species are known and how many may exist.
summary: About 1.5 million animal species have been described (IUCN, 2025). A 2011 estimate by Mora and colleagues puts all animal species at about 7.8 million, so most are still unnamed.

cards.headline: Scientists have named about 1.5 million animal species. Easy part.
cards.body: Every named species has a description behind it: someone found it, studied it and published it. But how do you count the animals nobody has found yet? One team came up with a clever answer, and it's humbling.

cards.fact: Named so far: about 1.5 million animal species.
cards.context: That's the IUCN Red List's 2025 tally of described animal species, and about 1 million of them are insects. IUCN itself warns that the figures aren't always up to date. So treat it as a snapshot, not a final score.

cards.headline: Counting the ones nobody has seen
cards.body: In 2011, Camilo Mora and colleagues spotted a pattern. Every species sits inside bigger groups, and those bigger groups are much better known. The number of groups at each level followed a steady relationship with the number of species, so the team used it to predict the total: about 8.7 million species of complex-celled life, give or take 1.3 million, and about 7.8 million of them animals.

mascot.line: Somewhere out there, an animal nobody has named is having a perfectly normal Tuesday.

cards.fact: Most animals have never been named.
cards.context: By Mora's estimate, about 86 percent of species on land and 91 percent in the ocean still await a description. Naming them all the traditional way could take up to 1,200 years and more than 300,000 taxonomists. It's an estimate, not a head count, but the message is hard to miss: you live on a planet you've mostly never met.

title: Backbone or Not
objective: After this level you can tell vertebrates, which have backbones, from invertebrates.
summary: Vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) have a backbone around the spinal cord. They are about 1 in 20 known species; invertebrates are the rest, many with outer skeletons.

cards.headline: Only about 1 in 20 known animal species has a backbone.
cards.body: Mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish: the animals on almost every poster. Together they're a thin slice of the kingdom. What exactly does a backbone do, and how does everyone else manage without one?

cards.headline: Your membership card runs down your back
cards.body: A vertebrate has a backbone: a column of bones called vertebrae, which partly encloses the central nervous system. Your spinal cord runs right through it. Vertebrates come in five familiar groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Run a finger down the middle of your back. Those bumps are your membership card.

cards.headline: No backbone, still sturdy
cards.body: Invertebrates are every animal without a backbone, from sponges and jellyfish to worms, snails, crabs and insects. Plenty of them still have a skeleton. They just wear it on the outside: most mollusks, crustaceans and insects have a hard outer skeleton that protects the body and gives muscles something to pull on. A beetle is a knight that never takes off its armor.

mascot.line: All those posters of lions and eagles, and the kingdom quietly belongs to the beetles.

cards.fact: About 95 percent of known animal species are invertebrates.
cards.context: Of about 1.55 million described animal species in IUCN's 2025 table, only about 76,000 are vertebrates. Britannica rounds more cautiously: more than 90 percent of living animal species have no backbone. Either way, we're the minority. And Level 2's million insects? Every one of them is on the other side of this line.

title: Naming Animals
objective: After this level you can explain scientific names and Linnaeus's system.
summary: Linnaeus gave each species a two-part name, genus then species; animal names start from 1758. Species sit inside ranks from domain down, and close relatives share a genus.

cards.headline: Say 'robin' in London and in Boston, and you mean two different birds.
cards.body: Early colonists in America named their bird robin because its breast color reminded them of the smaller European robin. The American robin is about 25 cm long, the European one about 14 cm. Same word, different animals. Scientists needed a better system.

cards.headline: Two words, one animal
cards.body: In the 1700s, Carl Linnaeus replaced long descriptive phrases with a two-part name for each species: first the genus, then the species. The European robin is Erithacus rubecula; the American robin is Turdus migratorius. Biologists everywhere accept the system, so a scientific name points to one species, wherever you are. Yours is Homo sapiens, and Linnaeus picked it himself.

mascot.line: A whole kingdom, and it all starts with one very long book.

cards.fact: Official animal names start in 1758.
cards.context: That's the year of the 10th edition of Linnaeus's Systema Naturae, the starting point for naming animals. Plants got their starting line a little earlier, with his Species Plantarum in 1753. Think of 1758 as day one of the official animal register.

cards.headline: Boxes inside boxes
cards.body: Linnaeus also stacked species into ranks: kingdom, class, order, genus, species. Biologists later added more, and today's ladder runs domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Close relatives share the lower rungs. Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars all sit in the genus Panthera, so the tiger is Panthera tigris and the leopard Panthera pardus. The genus works like a surname.

title: Warm- and Cold-Blooded
objective: After this level you can explain how different animals control their body temperature.
summary: Endotherms (mammals, birds) make their own heat; ectotherms take it from their surroundings and manage it by behavior. "Cold-blooded" is misleading, and inside heat costs food.

cards.headline: Some 'cold-blooded' lizards run hotter than some mammals.
cards.body: Britannica calls the words warm-blooded and cold-blooded imprecise and misleading, and that lizard is why. So if blood temperature isn't the real difference, what is?

cards.headline: Inside heat, outside heat
cards.body: The real difference is where the heat comes from. Endotherms make most of it inside their bodies and hold a steady temperature whatever the weather: about 37 °C for mammals and about 40 °C for birds. Ectotherms absorb most of their heat from their surroundings; that includes fish, amphibians, reptiles and invertebrates. Endo means inside, ecto means outside. The name tells you where the furnace is.

cards.headline: A lizard's working day
cards.body: An ectotherm isn't helpless. A reptile basks in the sun or lies on a warm surface to heat up, then moves between sun and shade, or turns its body, to control how much heat it gains or loses. Its temperature still rises and falls with its surroundings more than yours does. It runs its thermostat with its feet.

mascot.line: Next time you feel starving, you know who to blame. The furnace.

cards.fact: Your steady warmth is paid for at every meal.
cards.context: Because reptiles don't keep a constant inside temperature, they have a low metabolic rate and need less food than warm-blooded animals of the same size. Many can survive long stretches without eating. Your 37 °C is a furnace that never switches off, and food is its fuel.

title: What Animals Eat
objective: After this level you can explain herbivores, carnivores and omnivores.
summary: Herbivores eat mainly plants, carnivores mostly meat, omnivores both; teeth give it away. The giant panda is in the order Carnivora yet eats mostly bamboo.

cards.headline: The giant panda belongs to the meat-eaters' order. It eats bamboo.
cards.body: Up to 16 hours a day of it. So is a panda a carnivore or not? It depends on whether you're asking about its family tree or its dinner plate. Start with the plate.

mascot.line: Say cheese. Actually, say what you ate. Your teeth already did.

cards.headline: Read the teeth
cards.body: Teeth give a diet away. Wide molars grind leaves; long, sharp teeth grab and rip apart prey. A raccoon, an omnivore, carries both toolkits: sharp front teeth for ripping apart mice and large molars for chewing plants. Hand a biologist a skull and they're reading a menu.

cards.fact: A plant eater with a meat eater's gut
cards.context: The giant panda is a mammal in the order Carnivora, in the bear family, and its digestive system is more like a carnivore's. It can't digest cellulose, the main stuff of bamboo, so it pushes a lot through: 70 to 100 pounds a day. Remember Level 4's ranks? 'Carnivora' is the panda's order. What it eats makes it mostly a plant eater.

title: Food Chains and Webs
objective: After this level you can explain how energy passes along a food chain.
summary: Energy enters food chains through producers and passes up through consumers, about 10 percent per step, so most ecosystems have at most five levels. Chains overlap into webs.

cards.headline: A blue whale's dinner starts with sunlight.
cards.body: In one ocean food chain, single-celled phytoplankton feed tiny shrimp called krill, and krill are the blue whale's main food. So how does sunlight end up inside a whale, and why does so little of it make the trip?

cards.headline: Who eats whom
cards.body: A food chain starts with producers, which make their own food, nearly all by photosynthesis from sunlight, carbon dioxide and water. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat the producers. Secondary consumers eat them, tertiary consumers eat those, and apex predators sit on top. Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria finish the job, turning dead plants and wastes into nutrient-rich soil.

mascot.line: A 90 percent tax at every step. No wonder the top of the chain is so exclusive.

cards.fact: Only about 10 percent of the energy climbs each step.
cards.context: On average, each level passes on about 10 percent of its energy. The rest is lost: some food can't be digested, a lot escapes as heat, and some living things die without being eaten. Start with 1,000 units in plants, and about 100 reach the herbivores and about 10 the animals that eat them. That's why most ecosystems top out at five levels.

cards.headline: Chains tangle into webs
cards.body: Real animals rarely stick to one chain. All the overlapping chains in an ecosystem make up a food web. Level 6's omnivores are one reason: a bear eats berries, like a primary consumer, and salmon, like a higher one. Draw every arrow, and your neat line turns into a net.

title: Ecosystems
objective: After this level you can explain how animals, plants and places form an ecosystem.
summary: An ecosystem is living things plus nonliving parts working together. When Robert Paine removed sea stars from a shore, mussels took over: the sea star was a keystone species.

cards.headline: A scientist pried sea stars off rocks with a crowbar and tossed them in the sea.
cards.body: On purpose. It was an experiment on the coast of Washington State in the 1960s, and what happened next changed how ecologists think about the places animals live.

cards.headline: More than a list of animals
cards.body: An ecosystem is a place where plants, animals and other organisms work together with the nonliving parts around them, such as rocks, temperature and humidity. It can be enormous, or as small as a tide pool, which is a complete, tiny ecosystem of its own. Every part depends on every other part, directly or indirectly. That's the claim. Paine went to test it.

cards.headline: The shore without its sea stars
cards.body: Robert Paine's carnivorous ochre sea stars ate mussels on the rocky shore of Mukkaw Bay. Within two years of removing them from one stretch, California mussels took over rock that had held anemones, sponges, barnacles, chitons, limpets and seaweeds. On nearby shore where the sea stars stayed, the mix survived. One hungry predator had been keeping room open for everyone else.

mascot.line: One sea star, one crowbar, one idea that changed ecology.

cards.fact: Some species hold the whole arch up.
cards.context: Paine called them keystone species. A keystone is the wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch that keeps it from collapsing. Take out the sea star and the shore's variety fell apart. Think back to Level 7's food web: one predator near the top decided who got room at the bottom.

title: The Smallest and the Largest
objective: After this level you can compare the smallest and largest animals alive.
summary: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have lived. The smallest known vertebrate is the Brazilian flea toad (about 7.1 mm); male fairyfly wasps are the smallest adult insects.

cards.headline: The biggest animal ever is alive right now.
cards.body: Not a dinosaur. According to NOAA, the blue whale, a mammal swimming in today's oceans, is the largest animal known to have lived. So how big is that, and how small does an animal get at the other end of the scale?

mascot.line: Six tons of shrimp a day. And you thought your grocery bill was bad.

cards.fact: Blue whales can grow to about 33 meters long.
cards.context: That's NOAA's figure for the biggest, in the Antarctic: up to about 110 feet, weighing more than 150 metric tons. Yet they live almost entirely on krill, and the biggest may eat up to 6 tons of it a day. The largest animal ever runs on some of the smallest food in the sea.

cards.headline: Smaller than a single cell
cards.body: A male fairyfly wasp is smaller than a paramecium, a living thing made of just one cell. Yet the wasp is a whole animal, built from many cells. Line it up against the biggest blue whale and the whale is more than 200,000 times longer. Same kingdom, same checklist from Level 1, wildly different sizes.

title: Checkpoint: What Makes an Animal
objective: After this level you can sort animals by backbone, body temperature and diet.
summary: Three questions sort most animals: backbone or not, inside or outside heat, and what it eats. Some answers change with age: gray tree frog tadpoles eat algae and debris, while adults eat insects.

mascot.line: Salad as a kid, bugs as a grown-up. Every frog has a coming-of-age story.

cards.fact: A gray tree frog switches diets as it grows up.
cards.context: As tadpoles, gray tree frogs eat algae and bits of rotting debris in the water. Adults mainly hunt insects and their larvae. So the diet question depends on when you ask: algae and debris when young, insects when grown. The other two answers never change. A frog is an amphibian, so it has a backbone, and it takes its heat from outside.

title: What Makes a Mammal
objective: After this level you can explain the features all mammals share.
summary: Mammals breathe air, make their own heat, have hair at some point and feed young milk, the feature Linnaeus named them for in 1758. About 6,800 living species (MDD, 2026).

cards.headline: Linnaeus named your whole class after milk.
cards.body: In 1758, in the same book that started Level 4's official animal register, Carl Linnaeus grouped you with cats, whales and bats. He called the group Mammalia, from the Latin mamma, the milk-producing breast. So what does it take to join the club?

cards.headline: The mammal checklist
cards.body: Every mammal breathes air with lungs, has hair at some point in its life and feeds its young on milk. It also makes its own heat: Level 5's endotherms, with mammals at about 37 °C. One more badge hides inside your head, where a chain of three tiny bones carries sound across the middle ear. Milk is the one that made the name.

mascot.line: A whale's baby pictures are its only hairy ones.

cards.fact: Many whales have hair only before they're born.
cards.context: Hair is a typical mammal feature, but in many whales it has disappeared except in the fetal stage. That still counts: the checklist says hair at some point in life, and a whale ticks that box before it's even born.

cards.fact: About 6,800 living mammal species
cards.context: The American Society of Mammalogists' Mammal Diversity Database lists 6,791 living species in its July 2026 version. Next to Level 2's roughly 1.5 million described animal species, that's less than half of one percent. It's a small club, and you're a member.

title: Big Cats
objective: After this level you can describe lions, tigers and the other big cats.
summary: Panthera cats (lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars) often roar; small cats' hardened hyoid prevents it. Lions live in prides where lionesses hunt; tigers, the largest cats, live alone.

cards.headline: Your house cat will never roar. It isn't shy.
cards.body: A lion's roar can be heard up to five miles away. A house cat can't make that sound at all, however big its attitude. The difference comes down to one small bone.

mascot.line: All that attitude, and the house cat is stuck with a meow. Life isn't fair.

cards.headline: The roaring club
cards.body: Level 4 put lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars in one genus, Panthera. These are the big cats, and they often roar. Smaller cats have a fully hardened hyoid, a small bone in the neck, and that stiff bone prevents them from roaring. Same family, different hardware.

cards.headline: A roar is a property line

The lionesses bring home the dinner; the roar tells every other lion whose ground this is. Think of it as a fence you can hear from the next town.

title: Elephants
objective: After this level you can describe elephants' trunks, memory and family life.
summary: Elephants are the largest land animals. The trunk is a boneless nose and upper lip. African families follow a matriarch, and older matriarchs are better at spotting strangers.

cards.headline: Scientists played elephants recordings of other elephants.
cards.body: In Kenya's Amboseli National Park, researchers played recorded elephant calls to family after family, some from friends and some from strangers. How a family reacted depended on one elephant. To meet her, start with the most famous nose in the world.

cards.headline: A nose that works like a hand
cards.body: Elephants are the largest living land animals, in three species: African savanna, African forest and Asian. The trunk is a nose and upper lip fused into one, with no bones inside and about 150,000 muscle bundles. With it an elephant smells, breathes, trumpets, drinks and grabs things. Imagine your nose and top lip merging, then learning to pick things up.

cards.headline: Grandmother is in charge
cards.body: African elephants live in female-led herds. The matriarch, usually the biggest and oldest female, leads her related females and their young. Adult males tend to roam alone or in loose all-male groups. In an elephant family, the family tree and the chain of command are the same drawing.

mascot.line: Respect your elders. Especially the ones who weigh several tons.

cards.fact: Older matriarchs know a stranger when they hear one.
cards.context: In the 2001 Amboseli study, families led by matriarchs aged 55 or more were far better at telling strangers' calls from familiar ones. Those families also produced more calves. The saying goes that elephants never forget. The science adds: it pays to have a grandmother who remembers.

title: Whales and Dolphins
objective: After this level you can explain how whales and dolphins are mammals that live in the sea.
summary: Whales and dolphins breathe air through blowholes, have some hair and nurse their young. Dolphins sleep half a brain at a time. Toothed whales include dolphins; baleen whales strain food.

cards.headline: Dolphins sleep with half a brain at a time.
cards.body: Scientists think it lets them keep coming up to breathe, even while they snooze. A dolphin spends its whole life in the sea and still has to breathe air. That's your first clue that it's a mammal.

cards.headline: The checklist, passed underwater
cards.body: Whales, dolphins and porpoises meet Level 11's mammal checklist, with no discount for living at sea. They breathe air, are warm-blooded, have hair at some point in life and feed their young milk. They breathe through blowholes, nostrils on top of the head. Every breath means a trip to the surface, and the nose is already on top: a snorkel they never have to pack.

mascot.line: Twenty months of milk. Try telling this one it's a fish.

cards.fact: A dolphin calf drinks milk for about 20 months.
cards.context: A bottlenose dolphin mother is pregnant for about 12 months. Her calf nurses for about 20 months and stays with her for 3 to 6 years. That's a long childhood on milk, and about as mammal as it gets.

title: Bats
objective: After this level you can explain how bats fly and find food with echolocation.
summary: More than 1,300 bat species make up about one-fifth of mammal species. Bats are the only true flying mammals, on hand-shaped wings, and many hunt by echolocation.

cards.headline: About 1 in 5 mammal species is a bat.
cards.body: The U.S. Geological Survey counts more than 1,300 bat species. Pick five mammal species at random and, on average, one of them is a bat. Two tricks set bats apart: they fly, and many of them see with sound.

cards.headline: A wing made from a hand
cards.body: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight. The wing is a modified hand: a thin, flexible skin stretched between long finger bones. Spread your fingers and imagine the skin between them larger, thinner and stretched wide. That's a bat wing, and the order's name, Chiroptera, means 'hand wing.'

mascot.line: Loudest party in town, and you're not on the frequency list.

cards.headline: Seeing with sound
cards.body: In echolocation, a bat sends out calls that bounce off objects and come back to its ears. The echoes tell the bat what's out there. Most of those calls are ultrasound, too high-pitched for you to hear. After dark, the air above you may be full of bat shouts you'll never notice.

cards.fact: Closing in, a bat speeds up its calls.
cards.context: When a bat detects an insect it wants to eat, it fires off a rapid series of calls to pinpoint exactly where the prey is. More calls mean fresher echoes, the way you'd glance more often at something you were about to catch.

title: Marsupials
objective: After this level you can explain how kangaroos and other marsupials raise their young in a pouch.
summary: Marsupials are born tiny and finish growing in a pouch; a red kangaroo is born after about 33 days at jellybean size. Most live in Australia and New Guinea; opossums in the Americas.

cards.headline: A newborn red kangaroo is about the size of a jellybean.
cards.body: Its mother is pregnant for only about 33 days. Then the tiny baby climbs, on its own, straight into her pouch. Welcome to the marsupials: mammals that finish growing up outside the womb.

cards.headline: Born early, finished in the pouch
cards.body: Marsupial young are born in an embryo-like state and keep developing outside the womb. The newborn makes its own way to the shelter, warmth and milk of the pouch. Not every marsupial has a full pouch; in some species the nipples are simply exposed. Either way, the milk is the point: part nursery, part kitchen.

mascot.line: Moved out, still coming home for meals. Sounds familiar.

cards.fact: A joey moves out at about 235 days, but keeps coming back for milk.
cards.context: A red kangaroo joey leaves the pouch for good at around 235 days old, then keeps suckling until about 12 months. Red kangaroos are the largest living marsupials, with males standing about 2 m tall. Not bad for a jellybean.

cards.headline: Not only in Australia
cards.body: Most marsupial species live in Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands. The rest live in the Americas, mainly South and Central America. The Virginia opossum is the only marsupial found north of Mexico. Its young are born after just 12 to 13 days, about 14 mm long, and climb into the pouch. Seen an opossum in North America? You've met a marsupial.

title: Mammals That Lay Eggs
objective: After this level you can describe the platypus and the echidna.
summary: The platypus and four echidna species are monotremes, the only mammals that lay eggs. They feed milk from fur-covered patches, not nipples. Young echidnas leave the pouch when spines grow.

cards.headline: The first platypus skin in Europe looked like a prank.
cards.body: Some naturalists suspected a hoax: a duck's bill attached to the body of a mole. George Shaw described the animal properly in 1799. The bill was real, and the platypus had a bigger surprise to come.

cards.headline: Mammals that lay eggs
cards.body: The platypus and the four living species of echidna are monotremes, the only mammals that lay eggs. The platypus lives only in Australia; the short-beaked echidna lives in Australia, and the long-beaked echidna comes from New Guinea. Every other mammal in this chapter is born alive.

mascot.line: Duck bill, eggs, and milk. The platypus refuses to pick a lane.

cards.fact: Milk, but no nipples
cards.context: A platypus mother usually lays one or two eggs and keeps them warm between her body and her tail; they hatch in about ten days. Monotremes have no nipples, so her milk seeps from two fur-covered patches on her belly, and the young suckle it there. Still milk, so still a mammal.

cards.headline: Moved out for being prickly
cards.body: A short-beaked echidna lays one egg at a time. It hatches after about 10 days, and the young suckles inside the mother's pouch for two or three months. Then its spines grow in and it becomes too prickly, so she moves it out to a burrow. Every parent has a limit. Hers is spines.

title: Primates
objective: After this level you can describe apes and monkeys and what we share with them.
summary: Primates have forward-facing eyes, flat nails and big brains. Apes, unlike most monkeys, have no tail. Chimps and bonobos, our closest relatives, differ from us by about 1.2% of DNA.

cards.headline: Monkey or ape? Check for a tail.
cards.body: A chimpanzee has no tail, so it isn't a monkey. Neither are you. Primates come in famous kinds, and you belong to one of them. But first: what makes any of them a primate?

cards.headline: The primate toolkit
cards.body: Primates' eyes face forward, so the two fields of view overlap. They have flat nails where other mammals have claws or hooves. And for their body weight, primates have bigger brains than other land mammals. Look at your fingertips: nails, not claws. That's your primate badge.

mascot.line: Next family reunion: bring the bonobos.

cards.headline: Apes: the tailless branch
cards.body: Apes are tailless primates, while most monkeys have tails. The great apes are gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans, and humans belong to the same family, Hominidae. So when someone calls you a monkey, you can correct them: ape, please.

cards.fact: Your DNA differs from a chimp's by about 1.2 percent.
cards.context: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives, both about 1.2 percent different in DNA. Gorillas differ by about 1.6 percent, and rhesus monkeys by about 7. But you didn't evolve from any primate alive today: humans and chimps share an ancestor species that lived millions of years ago. Cousins, not grandparents.

title: Wolves and Dogs
objective: After this level you can explain how wolves became dogs.
summary: Dogs came from an ancient wolf population, at least 15,000 years ago; where and how often is debated. A puppy buried at Oberkassel about 14,000 years ago is the earliest known pet.

cards.headline: About 14,000 years ago, someone nursed a very sick puppy.
cards.body: It caught canine distemper at about 19 weeks old and was gravely ill. It lived to about 28 weeks, likely only because people cared for it. How did an animal descended from wolves end up in human arms?

cards.headline: Not today's wolves
cards.body: Dogs came from the gray wolf. But a 2014 genome study found dogs and today's wolves share a common ancestor that lived 9,000 to 34,000 years ago. Dogs came from an ancient wolf population that isn't well represented by any wolves alive now. Your dog and a modern wolf are cousins, not parent and child.

mascot.line: A mystery with fur, four legs and 72 ancient genomes. Detectives, fetch!

cards.headline: When and where? Still argued
cards.body: A 2022 study of 72 ancient wolf genomes put the change in the Ice Age, at least 15,000 years ago. Dogs matched ancient wolves from eastern Eurasia best: an eastern source fed all dogs, and a more westerly one fed some. Where it happened, and whether once or more, is still unknown. Humanity's oldest friendship has no birth certificate.

cards.fact: The oldest known pet was a puppy.
cards.context: The Oberkassel puppy was buried in Germany with a man and a woman about 14,000 years ago. Researchers call it the earliest known evidence of dogs being treated as pets. Someone sat up with a sick puppy long before anyone wrote a word. Some things haven't changed.

title: What Makes a Bird
objective: After this level you can explain feathers, beaks and hollow bones.
summary: Feathers set birds apart from every other animal. Birds also have toothless beaks, lay hard-shelled eggs and make their own heat, and big fliers carry bones partly filled with air.

cards.headline: A frigatebird's skeleton weighs less than its feathers.
cards.body: That's a bird with a seven-foot wingspan, and its bones are outweighed by its coat. It sounds like a trick. It's actually a clue to what a bird is, and to how so many of them manage to be so light.

cards.headline: Feathers are the password
cards.body: Not every bird can fly, so flight can't be the test. The real password is feathers. Britannica calls them the major characteristic that sets birds apart from all other animals. A turtle has a beak, but no turtle has a single feather. If it grows feathers, it's a bird. Full stop.

cards.headline: The rest of the kit
cards.body: Every bird is a vertebrate, one of the five backbone groups from Level 3. Its beak is its upper and lower jaws wrapped in a horny sheath, and no bird has teeth. Every bird lays hard-shelled eggs. And like you, birds make their own heat (Level 5), holding steady at about 40 °C. Feathers, beak, eggs, inner furnace: that's the kit.

mascot.line: Light bones, heavy coat. It's the exact opposite of how I pack for a trip.

cards.fact: In big fliers, the bones are partly air.
cards.context: In the largest flying birds, part of the bone is replaced by air spaces. A hollow tube can buckle, though, so the big wing bones carry struts inside, like the cross-braces in a bridge. That's how a frigatebird with a seven-foot wingspan ends up with a skeleton lighter than its feathers.

title: How Birds Fly
objective: After this level you can explain how wings create lift.
summary: A wing makes lift by turning the air flowing past it, which pushes back the opposite way. A bird's wing is also its propeller, and big breast muscles anchored to a keel drive it.

cards.headline: A bird's wing is a wing and a propeller at once.
cards.body: That's how Britannica puts it. One limb holds the bird up and drives it forward at the same time. So how does a feathered arm do two jobs, and where does the power come from?

cards.headline: Lift: turn the air down, go up
cards.body: Lift happens when a wing turns the air flowing past it. Bend that flow downward, and the air pushes the wing the opposite way: up. That's Newton's third law, action and reaction. Both the top and the bottom of the wing help turn the flow. Hold your flat hand out of a car window, tip it up a little, and you'll feel it.

cards.headline: Inner wing lifts, wing tip pulls
cards.body: A bird splits the two jobs along the length of the wing. The inner part, near the body, supplies most of the lifting surface. The wing tip supplies most of the propelling force, pulling the bird forward on every beat. Shoulder end: wing. Far end: propeller.

mascot.line: Flapping your arms won't work. You'd need a keel first. And, admittedly, feathers.

cards.fact: The power comes from the breast.
cards.context: Flying birds have a keel, a ridge on the breastbone that anchors the flight muscles. The big pectoralis pulls the wings down on the power stroke. A smaller muscle, the supracoracoideus, about one-fifth its size, raises them again. Feathers shape the wing; the breast makes it beat.

title: Eggs and Nests
objective: After this level you can explain how birds build nests and hatch their eggs.
summary: Nests range from nothing at all to woven weaver homes. The warmth comes from the parent's bare brood patch, near 38 °C, and the chick breaks out with an egg tooth it soon loses.

cards.headline: Some bird nests weigh more than a ton. Some birds build none.
cards.body: Falcons, owls and many seabirds and shorebirds make no real nest at all. Weavers weave grass into elaborate flask-shaped homes. Every bird lays hard-shelled eggs, though. So what does an egg actually need from its parents?

cards.headline: A nest is a cradle, not a heater
cards.body: Birds build with whatever works: twigs, leaves, mud, feathers, even spiderwebs. Some swifts glue theirs together with saliva. Nests run from about 2 cm across for small hummingbirds to more than 2 m for large eagles. But a nest only holds the eggs. The warmth has to come from somewhere else.

cards.headline: The bare patch
cards.body: Near the end of egg-laying, a sitting bird loses the feathers from a patch of its belly. This brood patch grows extra blood vessels that bring hot blood right to the skin, pressed against the eggs. Most birds incubate at around 38 °C, raising or lowering their body to adjust, and they turn the eggs as they develop. If both parents sit, both may grow a patch.

mascot.line: A tooth you only need once, for the world's hardest front door. Very efficient.

cards.fact: A chick breaks out with a 'tooth' it soon loses.
cards.context: The egg tooth is a hard tip on the chick's bill; ornithologist William Yarrell discovered its role in 1826. The chick uses it to punch the first hole in the shell. In most birds it falls off a few days after hatching, and in perching birds like finches and sparrows it's absorbed into the bill. Remember, no bird has teeth. This one is a loaner.

title: Birds of Prey

cards.body: Her name was Frightful, a trained peregrine, diving from nearly three miles up. She belongs to a group of birds built for one job: catching other animals. What turns a bird into a hunter?

cards.headline: Hooks and talons
cards.body: All birds of prey have hook-tipped beaks and sharp, curved claws called talons. The daytime hunters (hawks, eagles, vultures and falcons) are also called raptors. The night shift belongs to the owls, and they get the next level. Spot the hooked beak and the talons, and you've found a bird of prey.

title: Owls
objective: After this level you can explain how owls hunt in the dark.
summary: Barn owls can strike prey in total darkness by sound alone. Lopsided ears find a sound's height, a dish-shaped face funnels sound in, and muffled feathers keep the hunt quiet.

cards.headline: In 1958, an owl caught a paper wad in total darkness.
cards.body: Owls are the night shift of the birds of prey. Researchers Payne and Drury let a mouse tow a crumpled wad of paper through a pitch-dark room. The barn owl struck the paper. It couldn't see it, and paper doesn't smell like dinner. So how did it know where to strike?

cards.headline: Ears that aren't level
cards.body: It heard it. A barn owl's ears are lopsided, one slightly higher than the other. A sound from below comes in louder on one side, a sound from above on the other, so the owl can tell a sound's height as well as its direction. That pins prey down in three dimensions. Audubon says barn owls are better at finding prey by ear than any other animal tested.

cards.headline: A face shaped like a dish
cards.body: All owls have a facial disc, a ring of short feathers around the face. The barn owl's heart-shaped disc is especially prominent, and it works like a satellite dish, funneling sound toward the ears. That face you find so cute is mostly hearing equipment.

mascot.line: Shh. The best hunter in the room is the one you can't hear.

cards.fact: Owl wings are built to hush.
cards.context: Owl flight feathers have comb-like serrations along the front edge that break up the air, a velvety surface, and a soft fringe on the trailing edge. Together they damp the swoosh of flight. That may help twice: the prey can't hear the owl coming, and the owl can keep listening to the prey.

title: Penguins
objective: After this level you can explain how penguins survive the cold and swim.
summary: Penguin wings became flippers, and dense, nearly airless bones cut buoyancy for diving. Waterproof feathers, fat and heat-saving feet keep them warm; emperor males fast on fat.

cards.headline: Penguins fly. Just not through the air.
cards.body: Penguins live only in the Southern Hemisphere, and their wings evolved into flippers that drive them through the water. So what does it take to rebuild a bird for swimming, and to stay warm doing it?

cards.headline: Heavy bones on purpose
cards.body: Remember Level 21's air-filled bones? Penguins went the other way. Their limb bones are denser than nearly any other bird's, with almost no air inside. Scientists usually read that as ballast: less buoyancy means diving costs less energy. Emperor penguins, the deepest-diving birds on Earth, reach about 550 m. A floaty skeleton would fight them all the way down.

cards.headline: Coat, blanket, heat-saving feet
cards.body: A penguin wears a dense coat of short, stiff, waterproof feathers that trap air. Under that sits a thick layer of fat. And its legs and feet carry a countercurrent heat-exchange system that keeps the heat it loses to ice and cold water to a minimum. Three layers of defense, and the feet are one of them.

mascot.line: Nine weeks, no snacks, Antarctic winter. Parenting, but on hard mode.

cards.fact: An emperor penguin dad fasts for 9 weeks in winter.
cards.context: Emperor penguins breed in the coldest, darkest months of the Antarctic winter. The male incubates the egg for 9 weeks without eating, living off a thick fat reserve. Penguins also huddle in large groups to share body heat and shelter from the weather. His fat is both his blanket and his pantry.

title: Hummingbirds
objective: After this level you can describe hummingbirds' speed and energy needs.
summary: A flying ruby-throated hummingbird's heart tops 1,200 beats a minute, and hummingbirds are the only vertebrates that can hover for long. Tiny and poorly insulated, they save energy at night in torpor.

cards.headline: A hummingbird's heart can beat more than 1,200 times a minute.
cards.body: That's a ruby-throated hummingbird in flight, according to the Smithsonian's National Zoo. At rest it drops to about 225. A human athlete working hard reaches only about 150. What kind of life needs an engine like that?

cards.headline: The only true hoverers
cards.body: Hummingbirds are the only vertebrates that can hover for a sustained time, parked in midair in front of a flower. They can fly backward, and even upside down. A ruby-throated hummingbird beats its wings about 70 times a second in ordinary flight, and more than 200 times a second in a dive. That's a lot of flapping just to stand still.

cards.headline: A tiny furnace with a thin coat
cards.body: Hummingbirds weigh just 2 to 20 grams, their feathers are poor insulation, and their metabolic demands are enormous. Remember Level 5: making your own heat costs food, which is why a lizard can eat so much less than a warm-blooded animal its size. A hummingbird is the extreme case, a tiny bird with a thin coat and a racing engine.

mascot.line: Full throttle all day, power-saving mode all night. Honestly, relatable.

cards.fact: At night, a hummingbird can nearly switch itself off.
cards.context: When a night is cold or food is short, a hummingbird can drop into torpor: a deep, sleep-like state with its metabolism slowed to a minimum and its body temperature very low. In a study published in 2020, a black metaltail hummingbird in the Peruvian Andes cooled to 3.3 °C, the lowest body temperature recorded for any bird or non-hibernating mammal.

title: Parrots and Crows
objective: After this level you can explain why parrots and crows are so clever.
summary: Wild New Caledonian crows make hook tools, and Betty bent a wire into one in 2002. Alex the parrot named objects, colors and numbers. Their small brains are packed with neurons.

cards.headline: In 2002, a crow named Betty bent a wire into a hook.
cards.body: She was in an Oxford lab, facing a small bucket of food at the bottom of a tube. Another crow, Abel, had taken the hooked wire, leaving her a straight one. It was only the crows' fifth time handling wire. So Betty bent her own hook and lifted the bucket out.

cards.headline: Toolmakers in the wild
cards.body: Betty's species already had a reputation. In 1996, biologist Gavin Hunt reported in Nature that wild New Caledonian crows make hook tools: hooked twigs, and stepped-cut tools snipped from the barbed edges of pandanus leaves. They use them to fish invertebrates out of dead wood. Hunt noted the tools were standardized, in distinct types. Not random sticks: a toolkit.

cards.fact: A parrot named Alex could name 7 colors.
cards.context: Scientist Irene Pepperberg worked with Alex, an African grey parrot, for about 30 years. Using English words, he learned to identify 50 objects, 7 colors, 5 shapes and quantities up to 6, plus a zero-like idea. He died in 2007, at 31. Not bad for a 'birdbrain.'

mascot.line: Small package, dense wiring. The bird brain was underrated all along.

cards.headline: Small brains, packed tight
cards.body: How do they do it with such small heads? A 2016 study counted brain cells in 28 bird species. Parrot and songbird brains held, on average, about twice as many neurons as primate brains of the same mass. Large-brained parrots and corvids (the crow family) matched or beat primates with much bigger brains in forebrain neurons. Calling someone a birdbrain may be a compliment.

title: Migration
objective: After this level you can explain how birds migrate thousands of miles.
summary: In 2022 a young godwit flew about 13,560 km nonstop on stored fat. Tracked Arctic terns fly about 70,900 km a year. Migrants steer by the sun, the stars and magnetism.

cards.headline: A young bird flew for 11 days without landing once.
cards.body: In October 2022, a juvenile bar-tailed godwit tagged B6 left Alaska and flew nonstop across the Pacific to Tasmania, Australia. No stops for food, water or rest. How does any bird pull that off?

mascot.line: No snacks, no naps, no landing for 11 days. I get restless on a two-hour train ride.

cards.fact: About 13,560 km in one go: the longest nonstop flight on record.
cards.context: That's 8,425 miles, tracked by a 5-gram solar-powered satellite tag. The U.S. Geological Survey calls it the longest documented nonstop flight by any animal. The fuel was fat: B6 fattened up on Alaska's Kuskokwim Delta before leaving, and some migrating birds double their body weight before a journey. The fuel tank is the bird.

cards.headline: The tern that follows summer
cards.body: The Arctic tern goes farther, just not in one hop. In a 2010 study, scientists fitted 11 terns from Greenland and Iceland with 1.4-gram geolocators. On average, each flew 70,900 km a year between the Arctic and the Southern Ocean, with a stopover in the North Atlantic: the longest round-trip migration ever recorded electronically. In 2016, Newcastle University reported a Farne Islands tern with an estimated 96,000 km round trip.

cards.fact: A tern's lifetime of flying could take it to the Moon and back three times.
cards.context: Arctic terns can live more than 30 years, so the 2010 study estimated a lifetime of migrations may top 2.4 million km. And they don't get lost: migrating birds can tell which direction they're flying from the sun, the stars and Earth's magnetic field. Sun, stars and magnetism: three compasses in one small head.

title: Checkpoint: Birds

summary: A bird's body is a flying machine. The ostrich dropped the flying: no keel, no flight, but fast two-toed feet, the largest living bird and the largest egg of any living bird.

mascot.line: Two toes, one very fast plan: leave.

cards.fact: The ostrich is the largest living bird.
cards.context: An adult male may stand 2.75 m tall and weigh more than 150 kg. It lives in open country in Africa, and it cannot fly. Instead, a frightened ostrich can run at about 70 km/h, on the only two-toed feet of any bird, the main toe built almost like a hoof. Its escape plan is its legs.

cards.headline: No keel, no flight
cards.body: Remember Level 22's keel, the breastbone ridge that anchors the flight muscles? Ostriches, emus and their relatives, the ratites, have a smooth, raftlike breastbone with no keel at all. With nowhere to anchor big flight muscles, they can't fly. Size still counts, though: the ostrich lays the largest egg of any living bird, about 15 cm long.

title: What Makes a Reptile
objective: After this level you can explain scales, eggs and cold blood in reptiles.
summary: Reptiles wear keratin scales that hold water in and lay amniotic eggs that carry their own water, so they breed on dry land. Four living groups, mostly ectotherms.

cards.headline: A reptile egg carries its own pond.
cards.body: Most amphibians have to lay soft, jelly-covered eggs in water. Reptiles broke that rule, and it freed them to breed on dry land. Two inventions did it: a skin that keeps water in, and an egg that does the same.

cards.headline: A raincoat that keeps the water in
cards.body: Run a finger along a lizard and you'll feel scales, a continuous coat of them over most reptiles. Their main ingredient is keratin, the same tough family of protein that builds your fingernails and hair. Scaly skin with keratin and waxy fats cuts water loss, and it was one of the key adaptations that let reptiles live on land. A reptile keeps its moisture sealed in.

mascot.line: Why lug your eggs to a pond when you can pack the pond inside the egg?

cards.fact: A reptile egg is a private pond with a lid.
cards.context: Inside, the embryo floats in the amnion, a fluid-filled sac that gives it its own watery world. Around it, a leathery or hard, calcium-based shell holds in water and nutrients. That egg freed reptiles from needing water to breed, so they can lay on dry land, while most amphibians still lay soft, jelly-like eggs in water. Some reptiles skip laying and give birth to live young instead.

cards.headline: Four families, one thermostat
cards.body: Today's reptiles come in four groups: turtles, the tuatara, lizards and snakes, and crocodilians. Together they number more than 12,500 species. Remember Level 5? Most reptiles are ectotherms, taking their heat from outside: they bask in the sun or lie on warm surfaces to heat up, then slip into shade to cool down. Scales, shelled eggs and borrowed heat: that's the reptile kit.

title: Snakes
objective: After this level you can explain how snakes move, hunt and swallow their prey.
summary: Limbless snakes move in four main ways, smell in stereo with a forked tongue and the Jacobson's organ, and swallow big prey whole because the halves of their lower jaw aren't joined at the chin.

cards.headline: A python can swallow a whole deer, with no hands to help.
cards.body: Snakes have no legs, no movable eyelids and no external ears. Yet in Everglades National Park, a wild Burmese python was found with an adult white-tailed deer inside it. Getting there, finding the meal and getting it down each take a different trick.

cards.headline: Four ways to go without legs
cards.body: Snakes have four main ways of moving. The classic is serpentine: the body bends into S-shaped loops, and each loop shoves against whatever it can find, like rocks, twigs or pebbles. Heavy snakes like boas often creep in a straight line instead, lifting, anchoring and pushing with their belly scales, caterpillar-style. Concertina and sidewinding, the one for sand, complete the set. Every pebble in the path is a foothold.

cards.headline: Smelling in stereo
cards.body: To find a meal, a snake flicks its tongue. Each flick grabs scent particles from the air or ground and delivers them to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of its mouth, which detects smells. The fork matters: each tip samples a different spot, so the snake can tell which side a smell is stronger on. It works like your two ears telling you where a sound came from. That flickering tongue is really half of a nose.

mascot.line: No knife, no fork, no chewing. Just very patient jaws.

cards.fact: A snake's chin comes apart.
cards.context: Unlike your lower jawbone, the two halves of a snake's lower jaw aren't joined at the chin, so they can spread wide and move independently. The snake walks its mouth over the prey, one side and then the other, while stretchy skin widens the gape. That's how most snakes swallow prey whole, even prey much larger than their heads. It's how that Everglades python fit a deer.

title: Venom
objective: After this level you can explain how venom works and how antivenom is made.
summary: Venom is injected; poison harms when eaten or touched. Venom's toxins attack nerves or blood. Antivenom comes from antibodies horses make against small doses of venom.

cards.headline: Calling a cobra 'poisonous' is technically wrong.
cards.body: Poison and venom are both toxins, and people swap the words all the time. The difference is how the toxin gets into you, and it's the key to how this level's cure works.

cards.headline: Who bites whom
cards.body: Venom has to be injected: a fang, stinger or spine wounds you and delivers it. Poison works the other way round. It harms when it's eaten or absorbed through the skin, so a poisonous animal, like a pufferfish, just waits to be touched or tasted. The rule of thumb: if it bites you and you get sick, it's venomous. If you bite it and you get sick, it's poisonous.

cards.headline: What's in the cocktail
cards.body: Venom is made in special glands, and it's a mixture of toxic enzymes and other proteins. Some are neurotoxins, which attack the nervous system; in a snakebite that can mean paralysis that stops a person breathing. Others are hemotoxins, which attack the blood and blood vessels, causing bleeding or wrecking the blood's ability to clot. A venom isn't one weapon. It's a toolkit.

mascot.line: The horse does the hard part. Its immune system learns the venom so ours don't have to.

cards.fact: Antivenom is still made with the help of horses.
cards.context: In the 1890s the French scientist Albert Calmette made the first snake antivenom, against cobra venom, and in 1895 began producing it with horses. The method has barely changed: a horse, or sometimes a sheep, gets small doses of venom, its immune system makes antibodies, and those are collected from its blood. WHO estimates about 81,000 to 138,000 people die from snakebites each year and calls antivenom the most effective treatment. If anyone is bitten, get medical help.

title: Turtles and Tortoises
objective: After this level you can describe turtles and tortoises and their shells.
summary: A turtle's shell is its own backbone and ribs, so it can't leave it. Tortoises are the land-only turtles. In sea turtles, nest temperature sets the hatchlings' sex.

cards.headline: You can't take a turtle out of its shell. The shell is part of the turtle.
cards.body: Cartoons show turtles slipping out of their shells like sleeping bags. Real turtles can't, and the reason is inside: the shell is built from the turtle's own skeleton.

cards.headline: A box made of ribs
cards.body: The shell has two halves: the domed carapace on top and the plastron underneath, joined along each side into a rigid box. The carapace is built from the turtle's backbone and ribs, fused to bony plates that form in the skin. So a turtle can never leave its shell, and it doesn't shed it the way some reptiles shed their skin. It isn't a house the turtle lives in. It's a ribcage worn on the outside.

cards.headline: Every tortoise is a turtle
cards.body: All tortoises are turtles, but not all turtles are tortoises. A tortoise is simply a turtle that lives only on land; other turtles live in fresh water or the sea. Together they make more than 350 species, found on every continent except Antarctica. Think of 'turtle' as the family name and 'tortoise' as the branch that never goes swimming.

mascot.line: The nest's thermostat is doing a job most animals leave to genes.

cards.fact: In sea turtles, the sand chooses boy or girl.
cards.context: Sea turtle eggs that incubate below 27.7 °C hatch as males; above 31 °C, as females; in between, a mix. That makes warming beaches a problem. A NOAA-led study published in 2018 found that 99.1 percent of young green turtles from the warmer northern Great Barrier Reef beaches were female. Hot sand, missing brothers.

title: Crocodiles

summary: Crocodilians lurk with eyes, ears and nostrils on top. Crocodiles: V-shaped snout, lower teeth showing. Alligators: U-shaped snout. Tongue salt glands let crocodiles go to sea.

cards.headline: Built to lurk
cards.body: Every crocodilian is shaped for ambush. Its eyes, ears and nostrils sit on top of its head, so they stay above the surface while the rest of the body hides underwater. It can watch, listen and breathe without showing much more than a bump. From the bank, a waiting crocodile looks like a log with eyebrows.

That's how the saltwater crocodile, the largest living crocodilian at up to 23 feet (about 7 meters), can turn up far out at sea.

title: Lizards and Chameleons
objective: After this level you can explain how chameleons change color.
summary: Chameleons are lizards that shift colour by tuning nanocrystals in skin cells (Geneva, 2015). Their big changes are social signals and help with heat, not background matching.

cards.headline: A chameleon's colour show isn't mainly about hiding.
cards.body: The idea that chameleons change colour to match their background is a popular misconception. Their fastest, brightest changes are meant to be seen. And in 2015, scientists worked out how the colours are made. The answer isn't paint.

cards.headline: Colour from crystals
cards.body: Chameleons are lizards, and like many animals they can move pigment around inside skin cells. But in 2015 a University of Geneva team showed their brightest shifts come from something stranger. Panther chameleons' skin cells, called iridophores, hold a lattice of tiny guanine crystals. Calm, the crystals sit close together and reflect blue. Excited, the chameleon loosens the lattice, and the skin reflects yellows and reds. The colour is tuned, not painted on.

cards.headline: Talking in colour
cards.body: So who is the show for? Panther chameleons make their fastest, most complex changes in social moments: a male facing a rival, or courting a female, often within a minute or two. Their colours also shift with light, temperature and mood, like fright, victory or defeat. What they don't do is repaint themselves to match whatever branch they're on. The fireworks are a message, not a disguise.

mascot.line: Blue for calm, bright for a rival, dark for a cold morning. A whole wardrobe in one skin.

cards.fact: A chameleon also dresses for the weather.
cards.context: Remember Level 5? Chameleons are ectotherms, so they rely on outside heat. Darker colours absorb more light, so a chilly chameleon can darken to warm up faster while it basks. Deeper in the skin, a second layer of larger crystals reflects much of the sun's infrared, which may help keep it from overheating. Its skin is a billboard and a thermostat at once.

title: Amphibians
objective: After this level you can explain how frogs and other amphibians live in water and on land.
summary: Amphibians live a 'dual life' and lay shell-less eggs in water. Their moist skin drinks and breathes, which let in the chytrid fungus; IUCN (2023) found 41% of species threatened.

cards.headline: A frog drinks through its skin.
cards.body: An amphibian takes in most of its water through its skin rather than by drinking, and it breathes through that skin too. That open, living skin is the group's great trick. It also turned out to be their weak spot.

cards.headline: A double life
cards.body: Amphibian loosely means 'dual life' in Greek, a nod to the metamorphosis many frogs and salamanders go through, starting life in one shape and ending in another. Most amphibians lay soft, jelly-covered eggs with no shell, in water or damp places: none of Level 31's packed pond. The class has three branches: frogs, salamanders and the legless caecilians.

cards.headline: Skin that drinks and breathes
cards.body: An amphibian's skin stays moist and permeable, kept wet by mucus glands. Water soaks in across it, and it's one of the animal's three breathing surfaces. Where a lizard wears a raincoat, a frog wears something closer to a wet lung. That works beautifully in damp places, and it leaves the skin wide open to whatever lands on it.

mascot.line: The very skin that lets a frog drink and breathe was the door the fungus walked through.

cards.fact: In 2023, IUCN found 41 percent of amphibian species threatened with extinction.
cards.context: That makes amphibians the most threatened class of vertebrates. From 1980 to 2004 the leading cause of worsening risk was disease from the chytrid fungus, which infects the skin and upsets the salts it moves into the body until the heart stops. A 2019 study linked chytrid to declines in at least 501 amphibian species, including 90 presumed extinctions. Since 2004, climate change has taken the lead.

title: From Tadpole to Frog
objective: After this level you can explain how a tadpole turns into a frog.
summary: A tadpole has gills, a finned tail and no legs. Hind legs come first, then lungs and front legs; the tail is absorbed. Gudernatsch (1912) showed thyroid hormone drives it.

cards.headline: A tadpole never drops its tail. Its body absorbs it.
cards.body: Somewhere between two months and three years, a swimming larva with gills rebuilds itself into a frog with lungs and legs. Here's the order of the work, and the chemical that gives the orders.

cards.headline: Barely a frog at all
cards.body: A young tadpole looks nothing like its parents. It usually has gills, a long, finned tail and no limbs at all, and it's often a plant-eater. Everything about it is built for life underwater: it breathes with gills where its parents will use lungs. To become a frog, almost every part has to be rebuilt.

cards.context: Friedrich Gudernatsch fed tadpoles bits of several horse organs. Only the thyroid gland sped up their metamorphosis. Later, removing a tadpole's own thyroid stopped the change entirely: without thyroid hormone, the rebuild never happens. Level 10's gray tree frog, algae-eater as a tadpole and insect-hunter as an adult, goes through this same hormone-driven makeover.

title: Dinosaurs Were Reptiles
objective: After this level you can explain what dinosaurs were and how we know about them.
summary: Dinosaurs were reptiles, named by Owen in 1842. They stood on pillar-like legs; pterosaurs and sea reptiles were not dinosaurs. Maiasaura's nests show eggs laid on land.

cards.headline: The first dinosaur was named mostly from a jawbone.
cards.body: In 1824, William Buckland described Megalosaurus from fossils made up mainly of a lower jawbone with a few teeth. Nobody yet had a word for the kind of animal it was. So what were these creatures, and how can we tell?

cards.headline: Terrible reptiles
cards.body: In 1842, Richard Owen studied the remains of three giant extinct animals and proposed a new group: Dinosauria. He built the name from Greek deinos, 'terrible' or 'fearfully great', and sauros, 'reptile' or 'lizard'. The reptile part was right. Dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles, in the same class as the turtles, lizards and crocodilians earlier in this chapter. Don't let 'lizard' fool you, though. Look at the legs.

cards.headline: Legs like pillars
cards.body: What set dinosaurs apart was how they stood. They held their legs straight under the body like columns, the way elephants do, instead of sprawled out to the sides like a lizard's. Their hip sockets even had a hole right through. Flying pterosaurs and sea reptiles like plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs were reptiles too, but on separate branches. Reptiles, yes. Dinosaurs, no.

mascot.line: Eggshells, tiny bones and worn baby teeth. The clues add up to a caring parent.

cards.fact: One dinosaur left a whole nesting ground.
cards.context: In 1978, a nesting site turned up near Choteau, Montana: nests with clutches of eggs, broken eggshells and baby dinosaurs. The babies were too young to walk, yet their teeth were worn, so someone was feeding them. Jack Horner and Bob Makela named the animal Maiasaura, 'good mother lizard'. Eggs in nests on land: the reptile plan from Level 31, preserved in stone.

title: What Makes a Fish
objective: After this level you can explain gills, fins and scales.
summary: Fish breathe oxygen dissolved in water through blood-rich gills, steer with paired fins and wear bony scales that grow all their lives. Most are cold-blooded; the opah is the warm exception.

cards.headline: A fish needs oxygen as much as you do. It just never comes up for air.
cards.body: Chapter 5 heads underwater, and the first animal to explain is the obvious one. A fish spends its whole life submerged, yet it breathes oxygen all day long. The trick is its gills. So what else, besides gills, makes a fish a fish?

cards.headline: Breathing water, sort of
cards.body: Water carries a little oxygen dissolved in it, the way soda carries its fizz. A fish takes water in through its mouth and sends it over its gills: fleshy filaments packed with blood vessels. As the water flows past, oxygen slips into the blood and carbon dioxide slips out. A fish doesn't drink its air. It sieves it.

cards.headline: Steering fins and bony armor
cards.body: Fins do the driving. The pectoral fins, the pair on a fish's sides, are crucial for steadying and steering, working with the fins on its back and tail to keep it balanced. Scales are the armor. On a bony fish, each scale is a thin plate of bone overlapping the next like roof shingles, and it keeps growing for the fish's whole life. The armor gets upgraded as the owner grows.

mascot.line: A warm-blooded fish. Somewhere, a biology textbook just sighed.

cards.fact: Most fish are cold-blooded. The opah breaks the rule.
cards.context: Remember Level 5? Fish sit with the ectotherms, taking their heat from the water around them, like reptiles and amphibians. Most fish species do. The opah doesn't: it is warm-blooded, and a heat-exchange system in its gills helps keep it warm. So even "fish are cold-blooded" is a rule with a footnote.

title: Sharks
objective: After this level you can describe sharks and their senses.
summary: Sharks are boneless, cartilage-framed fish older than trees. NOAA counts eight senses, from a sharp nose to a lateral line that feels pressure changes. Bites are rare: 65 unprovoked worldwide in 2025.

cards.headline: Sharks are older than trees.
cards.body: Sharks have been around for about 400 million years. The earliest trees showed up around 350 million years ago. So sharks were cruising the seas before the first forest cast a shadow. What is an animal that old built from, and how does it find its food?

cards.headline: A skeleton you could bend
cards.body: Sharks are fish, but they have no bones at all. Remember Level 41's bony fish, with scales of bone? Sharks are the other kind: cartilaginous fishes. Their whole skeleton is cartilage, the lightweight, flexible stuff that shapes your ear. Fold your ear over and let go. That's shark skeleton material.

cards.headline: Eight senses
cards.body: NOAA counts eight shark senses. Five are ones you have too: sight, hearing, smell, touch and taste. A shark's nose is famously sharp; it can smell blood in the water from a long way off. Then there's the lateral line, a row of tiny pores running from snout to tail. As water flows through them, sensory cells pick up changes in pressure. A shark feels the water around it move.

mascot.line: Older than trees and still not very interested in people. Honestly, fair.

cards.fact: Shark bites are rare: 65 unprovoked bites worldwide in 2025.
cards.context: That count comes from the International Shark Attack File, which tracks bites around the world. The 2025 total was in line with the average of 61 a year from 2020 to 2024, and the File calls the number extremely low. Eight senses tuned for finding food, 400 million years of practice, and people are still very rarely on the menu.

title: The Deep Sea
objective: After this level you can describe animals that live in the dark deep ocean.
summary: Below about 1,000 meters no sunlight reaches, and food is scarce so far from the sunlit plankton. Most deep animals make their own light; female anglerfish fish with a lure lit by bacteria.

cards.headline: Below 1,000 meters, the sun never shows up.
cards.body: No dawn, no dusk, just dark water all the way down. Yet the deep sea isn't pitch black. Something down there is making its own light. Who lives in a place like that, and what do they eat?

cards.headline: A long way from lunch
cards.body: Remember Level 7? Every food chain starts with producers, and producers need sunlight. In the ocean, that means plankton near the bright surface. Down in the midnight zone, it's dark, cold and crushed by pressure, and it's a very long way from the bottom of the food chain. That distance limits how much life the deep can hold. Down here, nobody can afford to miss a meal.

cards.fact: In one deep-sea survey, three quarters of the animals could glow.
cards.context: In 2017, MBARI scientists Severine Martini and Steve Haddock tallied the animals in Monterey Bay, from the surface down to 4,000 meters. Three quarters of them can make their own light, a trick called bioluminescence. In water the sun never reaches past 1,000 meters, the animals bring their own lamps.

mascot.line: Bring your own light and your own bait. The anglerfish packs for every occasion.

cards.headline: A fishing rod with a night-light
cards.body: Meet the anglerfish. Adult females of most species carry a lure, the esca, dangling from a "fishing rod" above the mouth. The glow comes from bioluminescent bacteria living inside it. Prey drift toward the light and find a big mouth of sharp, backward-pointing teeth waiting. It's fishing, with the bait built in.

title: Octopuses
objective: After this level you can explain why octopuses are so intelligent.
summary: The common octopus has about 500 million neurons, two thirds of them in its arms, and it solves puzzles and remembers the answers. It also has three hearts and blue, copper-based blood.

cards.headline: Most of an octopus's neurons aren't in its head.
cards.body: About two thirds of them are in its arms. Imagine your hands holding most of your thinking. How does an animal built like that end up so clever?

cards.headline: Brains in the arms
cards.body: The common octopus has about 500 million neurons, roughly as many as a dog. About two thirds of them sit in its arms, not its head. That lets an arm work on a problem while the central brain handles other tasks. Every arm gets its own assistant, and the boss gets some peace and quiet.

cards.headline: What a clever octopus can do
cards.body: Scientists have watched octopuses figure out how to open a clamshell that was wired shut. They find their way through mazes, solve problems, and remember the solutions afterward. Once an octopus has cracked a puzzle, it keeps the answer. That memory is the difference between lucky and smart.

mascot.line: Three hearts and blue blood. The octopus is basically royalty with a backup plan.

cards.fact: Three hearts, and blood that runs blue.
cards.context: Two of an octopus's hearts pump blood past its gills. Remember Level 41? That's where blood picks up oxygen from the water, just as it does in a fish. The third heart sends the oxygen-rich blood to the organs and muscles, and it stops beating when the octopus swims. The blood is blue because its oxygen carrier, hemocyanin, uses copper instead of the iron in your hemoglobin.

title: Jellyfish
objective: After this level you can describe jellyfish and how they sting.
summary: A jellyfish is about 95 percent water, with no brain, heart or blood: a nerve net and one opening do the job. It stings with nematocysts, harpoons that fire in about 700 nanoseconds.

cards.headline: A jellyfish is about 95 percent water.
cards.body: No brain. No heart. Not even blood. It's close to a bag of seawater with a plan. So how does something that simple catch its dinner?

cards.headline: Simple, not sloppy
cards.body: A jellyfish senses its world with a nerve net, a simple web of nerves instead of a brain. Its gut is just as minimal: one cavity works as both stomach and intestine, and a single opening serves as both mouth and anus. Everything goes in and out the same door. Economical, if not elegant.

cards.headline: Harpoons on a hair trigger
cards.body: The hunting happens in stinging capsules called nematocysts. Each holds a tiny harpoon, coiled up and waiting. Trigger them and hundreds fire at once. Each jab lasts about 700 nanoseconds and hits hard enough to pierce a crustacean's shell. That's how an animal without a brain gets through armor.

mascot.line: Proof that a very short to-do list can still get the job done.

cards.fact: No brain, no heart, still an animal.
cards.context: Run a jellyfish through Level 1's checklist. Many cells, no cell walls: check. Eats other living things: check, caught with harpoons. Level 1 put jellyfish on the animal map for exactly these reasons. The checklist never asked for a brain, a heart or blood.

title: Coral Is an Animal
objective: After this level you can explain that corals are colonies of tiny animals.
summary: A coral is a colony of tiny polyps that build limestone skeletons and catch food with stinging cells, so they are animals. Their algae are food and color; stressed corals expel them and bleach.

cards.headline: A coral is not a plant. It's a crowd of tiny animals.
cards.body: Corals stay fixed to the ocean floor, so plenty of people take them for plants. Remember Level 1's sponges, long mistaken for plants too? Corals pull the same trick. Here's who really lives inside.

cards.headline: A colony the size of nickels
cards.body: Most of what we call a coral is hundreds to thousands of tiny animals called polyps. Each is soft-bodied, most no thicker than a nickel, and each builds a hard outer skeleton of limestone. Polyps catch food with tentacles armed with nematocysts, the same stingers you met on Level 45's jellyfish, their relatives. They catch their food instead of making it. That's what makes them animals.

cards.headline: Roommates that pay rent in food
cards.body: Most corals share their tissues with microscopic algae called zooxanthellae. The coral gives them shelter. The algae photosynthesize and hand over food, so much that they are the coral's main food source. They also give the coral its color. Those famous reef colors come mostly from the tenants.

mascot.line: White doesn't mean dead, but it does mean trouble. Think of a coral running on empty.

cards.fact: Stressed corals throw out their algae and turn completely white.
cards.context: That's coral bleaching. Changes in temperature, light or nutrients can cause it, and NOAA names rising ocean temperature from climate change as the leading cause. Without its algae, a coral loses its main food and its color. A bleached coral isn't dead yet: if the stress eases, it can recover. If the stress drags on, the coral eventually dies.

title: Salmon Runs
objective: After this level you can explain how salmon return to the rivers where they hatched.
summary: Sockeye hatch in fresh water, grow at sea, then swim upstream to spawn where they were born, guided by the remembered smell of home. They die within weeks, and their bodies feed the river.

cards.headline: A sockeye salmon swims many miles upstream to spawn where it was born.
cards.body: It hatched in fresh water, spent years at sea, and now it's heading home, usually to the very stream or lake where its life began. It has no map and no one to follow. How does it find the way?

mascot.line: Imagine finding your childhood home by smell alone. Salmon never need to ask for directions.

cards.headline: Following its nose home
cards.body: Before a young salmon leaves for the sea, it learns the particular smell of its home stream. Scientists call this imprinting. Years later, the grown fish uses those odor memories to steer home. Salmon also imprint on Earth's magnetic field at the spot where they first reach the sea, a second clue for the long trip back. Home, for a salmon, is a smell it never forgets.

cards.fact: A salmon's last trip feeds the next generation.
cards.context: All sockeye die within a few weeks of spawning. Bears and eagles feast on them along the way; Level 6's bears are omnivores, eating berries and salmon. What's left of the dead fish gives energy and nutrients to the river, helping newly hatched salmon grow and survive. Bear, salmon, river, young salmon: one strand of Level 7's food web.

title: Tide Pools
objective: After this level you can describe tide pool animals like starfish and crabs.
summary: Tide pools sit in the intertidal zone, flooded and drained twice a day. Residents seal up or move to stay wet; hermit crabs reuse shells. Sea stars walk on tube feet and eat with an outside stomach.

cards.headline: Twice a day, the sea leaves. Some animals stay behind.
cards.body: On a rocky shore, the tide floods the middle of the beach and then drains away, twice every day. The animals that live there have to survive two worlds: underwater, then out in the air. How do they do it?

cards.headline: Life between the tides
cards.body: The intertidal zone is the strip where ocean meets land, between high tide and low. Level 8 called a tide pool a complete tiny ecosystem, and its residents each have a low-tide plan. Some close up inside their shells to stay moist and keep predators out. Others move down to water that stays put. Hermit crabs reuse empty shells as homes. Nobody here wastes a good shell.

cards.headline: The star that isn't a fish
cards.body: Sea stars live in the middle zone, beside the anemones. Despite the nickname "starfish," they aren't fish: no gills, no scales, no fins. (Check them against Level 41.) They glide on tiny tube feet on their undersides, which also grip their prey. And if a sea star loses an arm, it can grow a new one.

mascot.line: Bringing your own stomach to the restaurant. Bold, efficient and a little rude.

cards.fact: A sea star eats with its stomach outside its body.
cards.context: Remember Paine's ochre sea stars in Level 8, eating mussels? Here's how. A sea star grips a closed mussel with its suction feet and pulls on the shell until it opens. Then it slips its own stomach inside and digests the mussel right there. Dinner is served in the shell.

title: Ocean Food Webs
objective: After this level you can explain how tiny plankton support life in the ocean.
summary: Plankton are drifters: phytoplankton make food from sunlight near the surface, and zooplankton such as krill eat them and rise each night to feed. The ocean makes roughly half of Earth's oxygen.

cards.headline: Every night, the biggest migration on Earth happens, and you've never seen it.
cards.body: Tiny drifting animals rise from deeper water to the ocean's surface to feed, then sink back down by day. Who are these drifters, and why does the whole ocean depend on them?

cards.headline: The ocean's drifters
cards.body: Plankton are living things carried by tides and currents, too weak to swim against them. The name comes from the Greek for "drifter." Phytoplankton are the plant drifters. Zooplankton are the animal ones: krill, young fish, and weak swimmers like Level 45's jellyfish. Most plankton are microscopic, but size doesn't decide it. Swimming does.

cards.headline: Level 7's chain, zoomed in
cards.body: Remember Level 7's ocean chain? Phytoplankton feed krill, and krill feed the blue whale. Phytoplankton make food from sunlight, so they stay near the surface. Most zooplankton graze on them, rising at night to eat. With only about 10 percent of the energy climbing each step, the base has to be enormous. The largest animal known to have lived depends on life too small to see.

mascot.line: Next time you see the sea, say thanks. Quietly. The plankton are working.

cards.fact: About half of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean.
cards.context: Scientists estimate that roughly half of the planet's oxygen production happens in the sea, mostly by photosynthesizing plankton. Like plants, phytoplankton take in carbon dioxide and give off oxygen. Marine life uses about as much as the ocean makes, but half of the world's oxygen factory is floating out there, too small to see.
