title: Insects
objective: After this level you can explain what makes an insect an insect.
summary: Insects have three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs on the thorax and an outer skeleton. About 1 million species are named; about 10 quintillion are alive at once.

cards.headline: Right now, about 10 quintillion insects are alive.
cards.body: That’s the Smithsonian’s estimate: a 1 followed by 19 zeros. Beetles, flies, ants, moths: they look wildly different, yet every one of them is built on the same simple plan. Learn the plan, and you can spot an insect anywhere.

cards.headline: Count to three, then count to six
cards.body: Every adult insect’s body comes in three parts. The head carries the eyes, the mouthparts and one pair of antennae. The middle part, the thorax, carries three pairs of legs and, in most adults, one or two pairs of wings. The abdomen holds the digestive and reproductive organs. So count to three, then count to six. Anything that fails either count isn’t an insect, however buggy it looks.

cards.fact: An insect wears its skeleton on the outside.
cards.context: Remember Level 3’s beetle, the knight that never takes off its armor? Every insect has an outer skeleton like that. It protects the soft body inside and gives the muscles something to pull on. Your skeleton holds you up from the inside; an insect’s holds it together from the outside. Armor this good has one catch, and Level 58 will show you what it is.

mascot.line: Somewhere near you, an ant is reading this over your shoulder. Statistically, several.

cards.fact: About 1 million insect species have names.
cards.context: Level 2 counted about 1.5 million described animal species, and about 1 million of them are insects. Then there are the individuals: the Smithsonian’s 10 quintillion. Treat both numbers as estimates, since nobody can census every ant in every forest. But whichever way you count, kinds or bodies, insects fill the animal kingdom.

title: Ants
objective: After this level you can explain how ant colonies work.
summary: An ant queen lays the eggs; sterile female workers do the rest; males only mate. Scent trails lead workers to food, and leafcutter ants farm a fungus on cut leaves.

cards.headline: Every worker ant you’ve ever seen was female.
cards.body: The ant hauling a crumb across your kitchen floor? She’s a sister, not a brother, and so is every worker in her nest. An ant colony runs less like a crowd and more like a family business. So who does what?

cards.headline: One mother, a nest full of daughters
cards.body: The queen’s main job is reproduction: she lays the eggs, and she may live for many years. Her daughters, the workers, are sterile, so they put all their effort into everyone else. They build, repair and defend the nest and feed the young, the other adults and the queen. Males turn up only to mate, and after mating, a male dies. It’s less a kingdom than a very busy nursery.

cards.headline: Follow the smell
cards.body: How does a whole line of ants find the same crumb? Some ants leave scent trails made of chemicals called pheromones, and their nestmates follow the trail to the food. That’s why ants so often march in single file: each one is following the path the ants before her marked. A trail of ants is basically a smell you can see.

mascot.line: Leaves in, lunch out. Tiny farmers with no tractors and a very long head start.

cards.fact: Leafcutter ants are farmers.
cards.context: They carry cut leaves home, but they don’t eat them. The leaves feed a fungus the ants grow in their nest, and the fungus feeds the colony. Their crop is found only with the ants, never in the wild. And they got there first: ants were farming fungus tens of millions of years before people began farming, about 12,000 years ago.

title: Bees
objective: After this level you can explain how bees make honey and pollinate plants.
summary: Honeybee workers turn nectar into honey with enzymes and wing-fanning, and build comb from their own wax. Pollen caught in a bee’s hairs rubs off on the next flower.

cards.headline: Honey is flower nectar that bees have dried out.
cards.body: A bee doesn’t find honey. She makes it, from nectar, using her own chemistry, her wings and wax from her own body. And while she’s out shopping for nectar, she does the flowers a favor they can’t do for themselves.

cards.headline: The honey recipe
cards.body: Back at the hive, enzymes break the complex sugars in nectar into simpler ones. Then the bees beat their wings to help the extra water evaporate, and when it’s ready, they seal each cell with wax. Finished honey is only about 18 percent water. It’s the world’s smallest drying room, powered by wings.

cards.fact: Beeswax comes out of the bee.
cards.context: The wax workers make comes from four pairs of wax glands on the underside of the body. With it, they build comb: two layers of six-sided cells, where the colony keeps its honey. And the builders are all daughters again. Like Level 52’s ants, honeybee workers are females that never reproduce.

mascot.line: Paid in nectar, delivers pollen, never asks for a tip. Best courier in the garden.

cards.headline: Pollen hitchhikes on fuzz
cards.body: Flowers can’t walk, so they need a courier to move pollen from a flower’s anther to a stigma. That’s pollination. A bee is a fuzzy courier: her dense coat of branched hairs catches pollen as she feeds, and some rubs off on the stigma of the next flower. Honeybee workers also pack pollen into baskets on their hind legs to take home. She gets food; the flower gets its pollen delivered.

title: Butterflies
objective: After this level you can explain how a caterpillar becomes a butterfly.
summary: Butterflies pass through egg, larva, pupa and adult. In the chrysalis most caterpillar tissue dissolves, and imaginal discs build the wings, legs and eyes.

cards.headline: Inside a chrysalis, a caterpillar digests itself.
cards.body: It releases enzymes that dissolve most of its own body into what scientists call caterpillar soup. Out of that soup comes an animal with wings, new legs and new eyes. So how do you build a butterfly from soup?

events.label: Egg: a monarch egg hatches about four days after it’s laid
Larva, the caterpillar: grows from under 1 cm to about 5 cm
Pupa, the chrysalis: the body is rebuilt inside
Adult: the winged butterfly climbs out

cards.headline: Soup with a blueprint
cards.body: The meltdown isn’t chaos. While the caterpillar was still inside its egg, it grew small groups of cells called imaginal discs, one for each adult part it would need: eyes, wings, legs and more. In the chrysalis, the discs survive, feed on the soup around them and divide fast. In a fruit fly, a wing disc can grow from about 50 cells to more than 50,000. The caterpillar carried the plans for its future the whole time.

mascot.line: Imagine carrying your grown-up self around as a tiny folded plan. Caterpillars just do it.

cards.fact: Four stages add up to complete metamorphosis.
cards.context: Going through all four, egg, larva, pupa and adult, is what biologists call complete metamorphosis. The caterpillar and the butterfly look like two different animals, but they’re one insect at two ends of the same process. The wings you admire were packed away as tiny discs inside the caterpillar.

title: Spiders
objective: After this level you can explain how spiders make silk and spin webs.
summary: Spiders are arachnids: two body parts, eight legs, no antennae. Silk is a liquid protein that hardens as it leaves the spinnerets; many orb weavers eat and rebuild their webs.

cards.headline: A spider is not an insect. Count its legs.
cards.body: Eight, not six. Level 51’s insect test fails on the legs, and it fails on the body parts too. Spiders are arachnids, a different group altogether. And every one of them carries a silk factory in its abdomen.

cards.headline: Liquid in, thread out
cards.body: Spider silk starts as a liquid protein made in glands in the abdomen. It leaves through the spinnerets, small silk-making organs usually on the underside of the abdomen, and hardens as it’s drawn out. Not every spider builds a web; some go hunting instead. But nearly all spiders are predators, feeding mostly on insects. Silk is their fishing line.

mascot.line: Eat the leftovers, then rebuild the kitchen. Honestly, admirable housekeeping.

cards.fact: Many orb weavers eat their own webs.
cards.context: Many orb weavers that hunt at night take down their web toward dawn, eat it, and build a fresh one each night. Eating the old silk sends its protein back to the silk glands to make new silk. An orb web takes about 30 to 45 minutes to build. It’s a fishing net you swallow every morning and knit again every evening.

title: Snails and Slugs
objective: After this level you can describe snails, slugs and their relatives.
summary: Snails and slugs are gastropods, the largest mollusk group. They glide on one muscular foot over mucus and eat with a radula of tiny teeth. Slugs lost their shells.

cards.headline: A slug is a snail that lost its shell.
cards.body: Not in an accident: over the course of evolution. In slugs, the shell has shrunk to a small leftover inside the body, or vanished completely. Snails and slugs are the same kind of animal, a gastropod, and they share some very strange equipment.

cards.headline: Meet the mollusks
cards.body: Snails and slugs are mollusks: soft-bodied invertebrates, usually wrapped wholly or partly in a shell made by a layer of tissue called the mantle. Gastropods, the snails and slugs, are the largest group of mollusks. Their relatives include clams, mussels and oysters, and also squids and octopuses. A garden snail and a squid are family, which shows how much you can do with “soft-bodied.”

cards.headline: Life on one foot
cards.body: A snail travels on its foot, a single muscular organ that ripples with waves of contraction. Land snails and slugs glide along on a track of mucus. That shiny trail across your garden path is the road a snail builds for itself as it goes.

mascot.line: Thousands of teeth and not one toothbrush. Snails really commit to the salad.

cards.fact: A snail eats with a ribbon of teeth.
cards.context: Snails and slugs eat with a jaw and a radula, a flexible band of thousands of microscopic teeth. The jaw cuts off a piece of leaf, and the radula rasps it down; covered in rows of tiny teeth, it’s coarse like sandpaper. So when a snail eats your lettuce, it isn’t biting it. It’s sanding it.

title: Earthworms
objective: After this level you can explain how earthworms help the soil.
summary: Earthworms breathe through moist skin, open burrows for air, water and roots, and leave rich casts. Darwin estimated they move over ten tons of earth per acre a year.

cards.headline: In 1881, Charles Darwin wrote a book about worms. It was a hit.
cards.body: It sold 6,000 copies within a year, and at first it sold far faster than On the Origin of Species had. Why would anyone rush to buy a book about earthworms? Because Darwin showed what they do to the ground under your feet.

cards.headline: Breathing through skin
cards.body: An earthworm has no lungs. It breathes through its skin, and that only works while the skin stays moist, so worms need damp soil. Its body is a chain of ringlike segments, as many as 150 in one common species. Most of the time you never see them. They’re noticed mainly after heavy rain, when they come up to the surface.

cards.headline: Plowing without a plow
cards.body: Earthworms eat decaying plants and swallow plenty of soil along the way. Their burrows open passages for air, water and roots, and they drag plant material down into the ground. What comes out the other end, the worm’s casts, is richer than the surrounding soil, with nutrients in forms plants can use more easily. Every worm is a tiny tiller and a fertilizer factory in one.

mascot.line: No lungs, no plow, and still the hardest-working farmhands around.

cards.fact: More than ten tons of earth per acre, every year.
cards.context: That was Darwin’s estimate for many parts of England: more than ten tons of dry earth passing through worms’ bodies and brought up to the surface on each acre of land, every year. His conclusion was a lovely one. Long before people existed, the land was already being plowed, by earthworms.

title: Crabs and Lobsters
objective: After this level you can describe crustaceans and their armor.
summary: Crustaceans have two pairs of antennae and shells stiffened with calcium carbonate. Armor can’t grow, so they molt and hide while the soft new shell hardens.

cards.headline: A lobster often eats its own old shell.
cards.body: Right after climbing out of it. It sounds like a strange snack, but it’s a smart move for an animal whose armor can’t grow. So how does a crab or a lobster get bigger inside a suit of armor?

cards.headline: Armor with minerals added
cards.body: Crabs, lobsters, shrimps and even wood lice, the pill bugs of the garden, are crustaceans. Like insects, they wear their skeleton on the outside, but a crustacean’s is stiffened with calcium carbonate for extra rigidity. Look at the head, too: crustaceans carry two pairs of antennae in front of the mouth, where an insect has just one pair. A pill bug is a land-going cousin of the lobster on your plate.

cards.headline: Growing means getting undressed
cards.body: A rigid outer skeleton can’t grow, so crabs and lobsters shed it now and then. That’s molting. The animal climbs out wearing a new skeleton that’s soft and flexible, stretches it by taking in water or air, and then it hardens. An American lobster molts about 20 to 25 times in its first 5 to 8 years, before it’s old enough to breed. Growing up, for a lobster, is mostly changing clothes.

mascot.line: Waste not, want not: the old shell becomes the building material for the new one.

cards.fact: A fresh soft-shell crab has to hide.
cards.context: Just after molting, a crab is extremely vulnerable to damage and predators, so it stays hidden or buried for a few days while its new shell expands and starts to harden. The shell keeps hardening for two to three months. A lobster speeds up the job by eating its old shell, which replaces lost calcium and helps harden the new one. Armor is great, until the day you change it.

title: Mosquitoes
objective: After this level you can explain why mosquitoes kill more people than any other animal.
summary: Only female mosquitoes bite, for egg-making blood. Bites carry germs such as malaria parasites; WHO estimated 610,000 malaria deaths in 2024.

cards.headline: The CDC calls the mosquito the world’s deadliest animal.
cards.body: Not a shark, not a snake: a small insect. Mosquitoes spread malaria, dengue, West Nile, Zika and more. The bite itself isn’t what kills. What rides along with it is.

cards.headline: Only the mothers bite
cards.body: Only female mosquitoes bite people and animals. They need a blood meal to produce eggs. The rest of the time, females and males alike sip flower nectar and fruit juices. So every mosquito that has ever bitten you was a female getting ready to lay eggs. The males were off somewhere, drinking juice.

cards.fact: A mosquito starts life in water.
cards.context: Female Anopheles mosquitoes, the kind that spread malaria, lay their eggs right on water. The larvae that hatch live in the water, and so do the pupae, which don’t eat at all. Only then does the adult emerge, and only the adult female bites. From egg to adult takes about 10 to 14 days.

cards.headline: The needle is shared
cards.body: Mosquitoes pick up germs, such as viruses and parasites, when they bite infected people or animals, and spread them with later bites. Malaria works this way. It’s caused by Plasmodium parasites, which reach people mainly through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. The mosquito is the delivery van; the parasite is the cargo.

mascot.line: Small animal, big consequences. This one is worth taking seriously.

cards.fact: Malaria killed an estimated 610,000 people in 2024.
cards.context: That’s the World Health Organization’s estimate, from about 282 million cases. About 95 percent of the deaths were in WHO’s African Region, and there, children under 5 were about three-quarters of them. That toll is why a tiny insect heads the CDC’s list.

title: Checkpoint: Insects and Other Invertebrates
objective: After this level you can compare insects, spiders, mollusks and crustaceans.
summary: Insects, spiders and crustaceans are arthropods, with jointed legs and outer skeletons: about 84% of described animal species. Snails and earthworms are built another way.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: one word links the bee, the spider and the crab.
cards.body: They look nothing alike. Yet all three share a family name that means “jointed feet.” The snail and the earthworm don’t make the cut. Let’s line them up and see why.

cards.headline: Jointed feet, and a crowd
cards.body: All three are arthropods: animals with a jointed outer skeleton made of chitin bound to protein, and a segmented body whose segments carry jointed legs. The name says it: arthropod means “jointed feet.” By Britannica’s count, about 84 percent of described animal species are arthropods, most of them insects. If you picked an animal species at random, you’d very likely land on one.

mascot.line: Joints, shells, slime or segments: the backbone-free crowd has tried every design.

cards.headline: Two outsiders without joints
cards.body: A snail has no jointed legs at all. It’s a mollusk: a soft body, often inside a shell its mantle makes, carried on one muscular foot. The earthworm has no jointed legs either: it’s a chain of ringlike segments that breathes through its skin. Same kingdom, same missing backbone, very different ways to build a body without one.

title: Adaptation
objective: After this level you can explain how animals are adapted to where they live.
summary: An adaptation fits living things to their home. The desert fennec fox's huge ears shed heat; the Arctic fox's small ears keep it in. Populations adapt over generations; individuals don't.

cards.headline: Two foxes, two very different pairs of ears.
cards.body: The fennec, a desert fox, has the biggest ears for its size of anyone in the dog family. The Arctic fox has short, rounded ones. Same family, opposite ears. That's no accident, and the reason is where each fox lives.

cards.headline: Radiators and lids
cards.body: Like every mammal, a fox makes its own heat and keeps about 37 °C inside. In the desert, the danger is too much of it: the fennec's huge ears help release body heat and keep it cool. In the Arctic, the danger runs the other way: the Arctic fox's small ears reduce heat loss, because less of it is exposed to the cold. One fox wears radiators on its head. The other keeps the lid on.

cards.headline: What an adaptation is
cards.body: Biologists call this fit an adaptation: an adjustment to the environment that improves an animal's chances of surviving there. It can be a body feature or a behavior, and the fennec has both. Thick fur on its paws protects its feet from hot sand, and it spends the heat of the day in a burrow, hunting at night. Ears, paws and timetable, all tuned to the same desert.

mascot.line: Wishing really hard for bigger ears has never worked. Believe me, I've checked.

cards.fact: No fox ever grew its own ears bigger.
cards.context: Individual animals can't adapt. Adaptation happens in populations, over several generations, as the result of natural selection acting on inherited differences. That process gets its own chapter later. For now, the result is what counts: animals that fit their homes.

title: Camouflage
objective: After this level you can explain how animals hide in plain sight.
summary: Camouflage hides animals: background matching copies color, shape or movement; countershading (dark back, pale belly) flattens a body; Arctic foxes change coats by season.

cards.headline: Some leaves go for a walk.
cards.body: A leaf insect doesn't just look like a leaf. When it moves, it rocks back and forth, like a leaf blown by the wind. Hiding, it turns out, is about more than color.

cards.headline: Match the background
cards.body: The simplest disguise is background matching: an animal hides by resembling its surroundings in color, shape or movement. Earth-toned deer and squirrels do it among trees, a flounder does it on the seabed, and walking sticks and walking leaves copy the plants they sit on. A predator scanning for dinner sees only more scenery.

cards.headline: Paint out the shadow
cards.body: Countershading is sneakier. The animal's back is darker than its underside, which evens out light and shadow so the body looks flat and harder to spot. Sharks use it in open water, where there's nothing to hide behind. Seen from above, a shark's dark back blends with the deep water. Seen from below, its pale belly blends with the bright surface. No background? Bring your own.

mascot.line: A new outfit every season, and it's still just trying not to be noticed.

cards.fact: The Arctic fox changes its disguise with the seasons.
cards.context: Remember Level 61's small-eared Arctic fox? Many are white in winter and grayish brown in summer, so the coat matches whichever season it's in. The white coat that hides a fox in the snow would stand out on summer ground, so it doesn't keep it.

title: Warning Colors and Mimics

summary: Warning colors advertise poison. Batesian mimics are harmless copies of dangerous species; Müllerian mimics are all harmful and share a pattern. The viceroy proved Müllerian (1991).

cards.headline: The viceroy butterfly was long called a harmless fake.
cards.body: It looks like a smaller monarch, and for a long time biologists thought that was a bluff: a tasty butterfly borrowing a poisonous one's look. Then someone asked the birds.

cards.headline: Bright means back off
cards.body: A monarch caterpillar feeds on milkweed, a poisonous plant, and the butterfly keeps the poisons in its body. Its bold pattern is warning coloration: a signal to predators that this animal is toxic or dangerous. A bird that has a bad experience learns to avoid the pattern, and then avoids other species that look similar too. Camouflage says "nothing here." Warning colors say "you'll regret this."

title: Hibernation
objective: After this level you can explain how animals survive winter by hibernating.
summary: Hibernation is a long, deep drop in metabolism and temperature; torpor is the short version. Arctic ground squirrels cool below 0 °C; bears cool a little, so their status is debated.

cards.headline: This squirrel spends winter colder than ice.
cards.body: A hibernating Arctic ground squirrel lets its core temperature fall as low as −2.9 °C, and it doesn't freeze. A black bear in its den cools by only about 5 to 6 °C. Both are famous winter sleepers. So which one is hibernating?

cards.headline: Turning the furnace down
cards.body: Remember Level 5: making your own heat costs food, and winter is short on food. Hibernation is the fix, a state of greatly reduced metabolism and lowered body temperature. A true hibernator can cool to near 0 °C, take only a few breaths a minute and slow its heart until the beat is barely detectable. It lives on stored fat in a protected den, and every few weeks it warms up and wakes briefly before settling back down.

cards.headline: Torpor: the short version
cards.body: Torpor is the same slowdown on a smaller scale: body temperature falls and the body's cells slow their work. White-footed mice and shrews use daily torpor that lasts just a few hours. A hibernator returns to torpor after each brief wake-up, again and again, for weeks. One is a nap. The other is the whole season off.

mascot.line: Five months without a snack or a bathroom break. Whatever you call it, I'm impressed.

cards.fact: Does a bear truly hibernate? Scientists still argue.
cards.context: Britannica says no: a bear's temperature doesn't drop much, and it wakes fairly easily. But in 2011, a University of Alaska Fairbanks team found hibernating black bears cut their metabolism to about 25 percent of normal, and called it hibernation. The bears go 5 to 7 months without eating, drinking, urinating or defecating. Judge by temperature and bears fall short; judge by energy saved and they pass.

title: Desert Survivors
objective: After this level you can explain how camels and other animals survive with little water.
summary: A camel's hump is fat, not water; it drinks up to about 30 gallons at once and can go nearly a week without. A kangaroo rat gets water from dry seeds and wastes almost none.

cards.headline: A camel's hump holds no water at all.
cards.body: It's fat. So how does a desert animal get enough water, and hang on to it? The desert has two famous answers, one very large and one very small.

cards.headline: The camel: fill up, then go
cards.body: The hump is a food store: fat to live on when food is scarce. Packing the fat into one hump also means the rest of the body isn't wrapped in insulation in the heat. Water is a separate trick. A camel can drink up to about 30 gallons (about 114 liters) in one sitting, then go nearly a week without drinking. It doesn't carry a tank. It just refills like a bathtub.

cards.headline: The kangaroo rat: barely drink at all
cards.body: A kangaroo rat eats mostly dry seeds, yet it has almost no need to drink. Digesting a gram of seeds gives it about half a gram of water, roughly one drop for every two seeds. Its breakfast is also its water bottle.

cards.headline: Spend almost nothing
cards.body: Making water only works if you don't waste it. A kangaroo rat neither sweats nor pants, and its kidneys concentrate its urine to an almost crystal-like consistency. It also spends the hot day in its burrow and comes out at night. The camel refills big; the kangaroo rat hardly spends any.

title: Polar Survivors
objective: After this level you can explain how polar bears and penguins survive the cold.
summary: Polar bears: thick fur over black skin, a fat layer, furred soles. Penguins: tight feathers trapping air over fat, and legs whose arteries and veins swap heat so the feet lose little.

cards.headline: Under its white coat, a polar bear is black.
cards.body: Its skin is black, and its fur isn't really white either: each hair is clear, with no pigment. The white look comes from light scattering in those clear hairs. So what actually keeps a polar bear warm?

cards.headline: Coat, fat and boots
cards.body: Layers. Thick fur is the outer coat, and under the skin lies a layer of insulating fat, topped up by eating seal blubber. Even the soles of its feet are furred, for warmth and for grip on the ice. A polar bear is dressed for the Arctic from head to paw.

cards.headline: The penguin's down jacket
cards.body: Penguins solve the same problem with feathers. Short, stiff feathers packed tightly together trap a layer of air next to the skin, and that still air does most of the insulating. Beneath it lies a thick layer of fat. Feathers outside, fat inside: the same two-layer plan as the bear.

mascot.line: Cold feet, warm heart. For once, that's a compliment.

cards.fact: A penguin keeps its feet cold on purpose.
cards.context: In a penguin's legs, arteries carrying warm blood down run right beside veins bringing cold blood back up, so heat passes across before it reaches the feet. An emperor penguin's foot skin stays near 0 °C, cold enough that it doesn't melt the ice it stands on. Warm body, cold feet, and very little heat wasted in between.

title: Shells, Spines and Stings
objective: After this level you can describe the ways animals defend themselves.
summary: Animals defend themselves with armor (the three-banded armadillo rolls into a ball), spines (porcupine quills detach in an attacker) and chemicals (a skunk warns, then sprays about 10 feet).

cards.headline: A porcupine can't throw its quills.
cards.body: It's a popular idea, but the quills are never thrown or shot. So how do they end up stuck in an attacker? This level's defenders don't hide or run. They make themselves very hard to eat.

cards.headline: Armor: become a ball
cards.body: The southern three-banded armadillo is covered in plates of leathery armor, and it can roll completely into a ball, shielding its soft belly inside. Only one other armadillo can do the same: the Brazilian three-banded armadillo. A predator that finds one is left holding a sealed box.

cards.headline: Spines: let the attacker take them
cards.body: A North American porcupine carries about 30,000 quills, attached so lightly that they come off easily in anything that grabs it. Cornered, it raises its quills, turns its back and lashes its tail. Once in a predator's skin, a quill keeps working its way deeper, about 1 mm an hour. The lesson lasts.

cards.headline: Spray: warn first, then fire
cards.body: A striped skunk gives notice: it stomps its feet and raises its tail. Ignore that, and it can spray about 10 feet (3 meters) with startling accuracy. The warning makes sense, because refilling takes about a week. Its white stripes are warning coloration, the same "back off" signal as Level 63's monarch.

title: Animals of the Night
objective: After this level you can explain how nocturnal animals find their way in the dark.
summary: Nocturnal animals hunt, mate or dodge heat and predators after dark. Many have big eyes and a tapetum lucidum, a mirror that makes eyeshine; tarsiers lack one and have huge eyes.

cards.headline: A tarsier's eye weighs nearly as much as its brain.
cards.body: And it has two of them. Why would a small primate build such enormous eyes? Because it works the night shift.

cards.headline: Why work at night?
cards.body: Nocturnal animals are active after dark. Some hunt then, some find mates, and many are avoiding the heat and the predators of the day. You've met two already: Level 61's fennec fox and Level 65's kangaroo rat both spend the hot day in burrows and come out at night.

cards.headline: Bigger windows
cards.body: Night is short on light, so night eyes are built to collect more of it. Many nocturnal animals have enlarged eyes with wide pupils. The tarsier, a nocturnal primate, takes this to the extreme: each eye weighs nearly as much as its brain. Big windows let in more light.

mascot.line: Next time a cat's eyes glow at you, it isn't spooky. It's recycling.

cards.fact: Eyeshine is a mirror inside the eye.
cards.context: Many nocturnal animals, cats and crocodiles among them, have a tapetum lucidum: a layer behind the retina that reflects light back for a second chance at being seen. That reflection is the glow you catch in headlights. Tarsiers have no such mirror, which is why their eyes had to be so big.

title: Senses We Lack
objective: After this level you can describe animal senses we lack, like sensing electricity.
summary: Animals sense what we can't: sharks and rays feel prey's electric fields, pit vipers sense infrared heat, sea turtles navigate by Earth's magnetic field, and reindeer see ultraviolet light.

cards.headline: A shark can find a fish hiding under the sand.
cards.body: It doesn't need to see it or smell it. It senses the fish's electric field. Your senses show you only part of the world, and plenty of animals perceive more.

cards.headline: Electricity
cards.body: Sharks and rays have ampullae of Lorenzini, sense organs that detect the weak electric fields around prey, even prey buried in sand. You have no electroreceptors at all. A fish can hold perfectly still and hide from your eyes. It can't hide from a shark's.

cards.headline: Heat
cards.body: Pit vipers, such as rattlesnakes, have a heat-sensitive pit between each eye and nostril. It senses the infrared given off by warm-blooded prey and helps the snake aim its strike, even in darkness. To a pit viper, a mouse on a cold night practically glows.

cards.headline: Magnetism
cards.body: Sea turtles use Earth's magnetic field to navigate their long migrations. In experiments, loggerhead hatchlings swam in different directions when exposed to the magnetic fields of different places along their route. They carry a built-in sense of where they are, no phone required.

mascot.line: Camouflage only works if the viewer's eyes play along. Reindeer don't.

cards.headline: Ultraviolet
cards.body: Reindeer can see ultraviolet light, which human lenses block. Against the snow, things that absorb UV look dark to them: lichen, their winter food, urine, and wolf fur. A wolf that blends into the snow for you stands out for a reindeer.

title: Checkpoint: How Animals Survive

summary: Heat, cold and predators each set a test that adaptations answer. Wood frogs survive about 65 percent frozen, with glucose keeping the inside of their cells unfrozen.

cards.fact: A wood frog spends winter partly frozen.
cards.context: Wood frogs winter in leaf litter and can survive with about 65 percent of their bodies frozen. First the liver fills their cells with glucose, a sugar that keeps the inside of each cell from freezing while the water outside turns to ice. Then the heart stops and the organs shut down. When it warms, the frog thaws from the inside out, starting with the heart.

cards.headline: Two opposite answers to the same freezer

title: Instinct and Learning
objective: After this level you can tell instinct from learned behavior.
summary: Instincts are innate, like a gull chick pecking its parent's red bill spot; learning changes with experience. Imprinting mixes both, as Tex the crane showed.

cards.headline: A whooping crane named Tex thought she was a person.
cards.body: Tex hatched at the San Antonio Zoo and grew up around people. As an adult, she wouldn't pair with another whooping crane. So in spring 1976, biologist George Archibald started dancing with her, because dancing is how whooping cranes begin mating. In 1982 she finally hatched a chick, Gee Whiz. How does a bird get so confused about who she is?

cards.headline: Born knowing
cards.body: Some behavior comes preinstalled. A newly hatched herring gull chick pecks at the red spot on its parent's bill, and the parent brings up food for it. Nobody teaches it that. Biologists call this instinct: innate behavior with a strong genetic component, no practice needed. Its big advantage is that there's no risk of learning it wrong. The chick doesn't need a lesson. It needs a red spot.

cards.headline: Learned on the job
cards.body: Learned behavior is shaped by experience, so it can change when the world does. Prairie dogs give alarm calls when danger comes near. But they learn to ignore human footsteps that never bring harm, while still calling at predators. Learning is flexible, and that flexibility is its whole point. A prairie dog that screamed at every hiker would never get lunch.

mascot.line: Somewhere a duckling is following a cardboard box with total confidence. Respect.

cards.fact: Imprinting: learning that has a deadline.
cards.context: In an early critical period, a newly hatched duckling learns to follow the first moving object it sees, whether its mother, a person or even a cardboard box. In 1935, Konrad Lorenz quacked like a mother duck at newly hatched ducklings, and they treated him as their mother. Tex had imprinted on people. Today keepers raise crane chicks in crane costumes, so the chicks imprint on cranes. No behavior is purely innate or purely learned; imprinting is both at once.

title: Animal Communication
objective: After this level you can explain how animals send signals to each other.
summary: Animals signal by smell (pheromones), sound, sight and touch. Vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and displays like bared teeth can replace a fight.

cards.headline: One monkey shouts, and the whole troop looks at the sky.
cards.body: Vervet monkeys don't have just one alarm call. They have different calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and the troop reacts to each one differently. Is that a scream of fear, or something closer to a word?

cards.headline: Four ways to send a message
cards.body: A signal is information one animal gives off that another can use to decide what to do. Signals travel by smell, sound, sight and touch. A pheromone is a chemical signal released to get a response from another member of the same species, to attract mates, sound an alarm or mark a food trail. Primates groom each other; a signal can be instinctive, learned or both. If someone reacts, it counts as a message.

mascot.line: Up for eagles, down for snakes, trees for leopards. Not bad for a vocabulary of three.

cards.headline: Leopard, eagle, snake
cards.body: In a 1980 study in Amboseli, Kenya, Robert Seyfarth, Dorothy Cheney and Peter Marler recorded vervet alarm calls, then played them back with no predator anywhere. The monkeys still did the right thing: they ran into trees at a leopard alarm, looked up at an eagle alarm and looked down at a snake alarm. Each call pointed to a kind of danger. The call alone was enough.

cards.fact: Some signals exist to prevent a fight.
cards.context: A dog bares its teeth to make another dog back down. Displays like this let rivals judge each other's fighting ability, so a weaker animal can back off before anyone gets hurt, and real fights happen less often. Some displays even overstate an animal's strength: a bluff. A snarl is cheaper than a scar.

title: The Bee Dance
objective: After this level you can explain how honeybees tell each other where food is.
summary: Bees do a round dance for nearby food and a waggle dance for far food: angle from up gives direction from the sun, duration gives distance. Von Frisch: Nobel 1973.

cards.headline: A bee finds flowers, flies home, and gives directions.
cards.body: Inside the hive, her sisters can't see the flowers, and there's no map on the wall. Yet after she dances on the comb, other bees know where to fly. Karl von Frisch worked out how she does it. So how do you give directions with your hips?

cards.headline: Two dances, two messages
cards.body: A forager with news of food dances on the comb while nestmates crowd around her. If the food is near the hive, she does a round dance, which sends them searching nearby. If it's farther away, she switches to the waggle dance: she runs straight ahead, waggling her abdomen, loops back to the start and repeats. The round dance says "somewhere close." The waggle dance gives an address.

cards.headline: The sun on the ceiling
cards.body: The straight waggle run is the map. On the vertical comb, straight up stands for the sun's direction. A run pointing straight up means "fly toward the sun"; a run tilted to the right of up means fly that far to the right of the sun. Distance is in the timing: the longer the waggle run lasts, the farther away the food. Clouds don't stop it, because bees can find the hidden sun using polarized light.

mascot.line: Even bees do better with a good dance teacher.

cards.fact: The dance won a Nobel Prize in 1973.
cards.context: Karl von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Konrad Lorenz, of Level 71's ducklings, and Nikolaas Tinbergen. The 1973 announcement called the dance genetically programmed and not learned. A 2023 study added a twist: bees that never got to follow experienced dancers made messier dances and got distances wrong. Practice helped, but they never got distance right. The steps are inborn; the polish is learned.

title: Packs and Herds
objective: After this level you can explain why many animals live in groups.
summary: Groups dilute risk and help hunters, at a cost. Wild wolf packs are families; the 'alpha' came from captive, unrelated wolves, as Mech showed in 1999.

cards.headline: The snarling "alpha wolf" came from wolves that had never met.
cards.body: The picture of a pack ruled by a top wolf that fought its way up came mostly from studies of captive wolves, such as Schenkel's in 1947: unrelated animals thrown together in an enclosure. Wild packs turned out to be something far more ordinary. First, though: why live in a group at all?

cards.headline: Safety in numbers
cards.body: If a predator takes one animal per attack, your odds of being the one shrink as the group grows. Alone, it's you. In a group of 100, it's 1 in 100. Animals in the middle of a group, like a fish school, are safer still, and a group that scatters unpredictably can confuse a predator. A crowd is the cheapest bodyguard around.

cards.headline: Teamwork, and the bill
cards.body: Groups help hunters too. Lions, hyenas and wolves that cooperate can corner and bring down prey more easily than one animal could. But group life has costs. Everyone competes for the same food, and if a group attracts too many predators, a single animal may be better off alone. Every herd is a deal that has to pay for itself.

cards.headline: A pack is a family
cards.body: In 1999, L. David Mech of the U.S. Geological Survey described wild packs as families: a breeding pair and their offspring from the previous 1 to 3 years. The alpha picture came from captive, unrelated wolves, who did form a pecking order. Mech had once used words like alpha himself. Now he says calling a wolf an alpha is like calling a human father one.

mascot.line: Top wolf turns out to mean "parent." Every family dinner makes more sense now.

cards.fact: In 13 summers, Mech saw no fights for the top spot.
cards.context: Watching a wild pack on Ellesmere Island, Canada, he found the parents simply lead. The mother mainly cares for and defends the pups; the father mainly leads hunting and brings food. Dominance displays showed up mostly over food, when parents steered it to the youngest pups. The "alpha" was just Mom or Dad.

title: Courtship
objective: After this level you can explain how animals attract mates, from bright feathers to birdsong.
summary: Often one sex chooses and the other competes, so showy traits spread. Courtship runs on signals: song, step-by-step displays and the bowerbird's blue bower.

cards.headline: A bird in Australia collects blue bottle tops to impress a date.
cards.body: The male satin bowerbird gathers blue things: bottle tops, drinking straws, clothes pegs, parrot feathers, flowers. He arranges them around a structure of sticks he built on the ground. Why would a bird go to all that trouble?

cards.headline: The chooser decides
cards.body: In many species, one sex chooses and the other competes to be chosen. Peahens are the classic choosers: they tend to mate with the peacock showing the brightest, most elaborate plumage. A trait like that can make survival harder, but if it wins mates, it gets passed on anyway. A peacock's tail is a love letter he has to drag everywhere.

cards.headline: Songs and steps
cards.body: Courtship uses the signal channels from Level 72. Birdsong tells listeners which species is singing and helps attract a mate. Visual courtship displays often run as a series of steps: one partner displays, the other responds. If a step goes wrong or the response never comes, the courtship is abandoned. It's a duet where one missed cue ends the date.

mascot.line: He builds the stage, then she builds the actual home. Classic.

cards.fact: A bower is a stage, not a nest.
cards.context: The satin bowerbird's bower is two parallel walls of sticks, which he even paints with chewed plant matter mixed with saliva. When a female arrives, he struts and bows with quivering wings, buzzing and rattling, often holding a decoration in his bill. If she mates with him, she leaves to build a nest and raise the young on her own.

title: Animal Parents
objective: After this level you can explain how animals care for their young.
summary: Care costs future young, so animals trade numbers for care. Orangutans raise only 4 or 5 young in a lifetime; seahorse fathers carry the eggs.

cards.headline: An orangutan mother may raise only 4 or 5 babies in her whole life.
cards.body: She has a baby only about every 7 to 9 years, and each one gets years of her attention. A seahorse father, meanwhile, gives birth to a brood and gives them no further care. Two very different bets on the same goal. Why?

cards.headline: Care has a price
cards.body: Every hour spent guarding one batch of eggs is an hour not spent producing the next. So parents face a trade-off: more young with little care, or fewer young with lots of it. Mammal mothers are locked onto the care side: they feed their young milk, and most carry them through pregnancy first. Parenting is paid for in babies not made.

cards.headline: The longest childhood
cards.body: Orangutans sit at the far end. Infants cling to their mothers from birth and can nurse until they're 6 or 7 years old. A mother has a baby only about every 7 to 9 years, so she raises just 4 or 5 in her lifetime. Daughters may stay close into their teens, watching their mother raise younger siblings. That's how they pick up the job themselves.

mascot.line: Dad does the pregnancy, then everyone swims off. Short parenting, very dramatic.

cards.fact: In seahorses, the father gets pregnant.
cards.context: The female places her eggs in a brood pouch at the base of the male's tail. He carries them for between 10 days and six weeks, depending on the species, then pushes the young out through an opening in the pouch. Care by the father alone is rare, but seahorse and pipefish males carry the eggs. Once born, the babies are on their own.

title: Tool Use
objective: After this level you can describe animals that use tools, from chimpanzees to crows.
summary: In 1960 Goodall saw chimps make and use termite-fishing tools. Sea otters crack prey with rocks; veined octopuses carry coconut shells for later shelter.

cards.headline: In 1960, a chimpanzee got humans to rethink what makes them human.
cards.body: Making and using tools was thought to set people apart from every other animal. Then, at Gombe in Tanzania, Jane Goodall watched a chimp she had named David Greybeard sitting at a termite mound.

cards.headline: Fishing for termites
cards.body: David Greybeard poked a stem of grass into the termite mound, then raised it to his mouth. Soon after, Goodall saw chimps pick leafy twigs and strip off the leaves before fishing with them. That was tool making, never seen before. When she told her mentor, Louis Leakey, he replied that we must now redefine man or accept chimpanzees as human.

cards.headline: Otters with hammers
cards.body: A 2024 study followed 196 radio-tagged southern sea otters in California. They use rocks, shells and even trash to crack open prey. Tool users, mostly females, could eat harder and larger prey and had less tooth damage, which matters: badly worn teeth can mean starvation. Researchers think females make up for smaller bodies and weaker bites this way, since raising pups takes a lot of energy. A rock is cheaper than a dentist.

mascot.line: Packing your house for later. That's planning, with eight arms.

cards.fact: An octopus that carries its house.
cards.context: Veined octopuses in Indonesia dig up coconut shell halves, carry them under their bodies while walking awkwardly on stiffened arms, and later join them into a shelter. A hermit crab's shell doesn't count as a tool, because it's useful all the time. The coconut only pays off later, once the octopus needs a hiding place. Reported in 2009, it was the first known tool use by an invertebrate.

title: How Smart Are Animals?
objective: After this level you can explain how scientists test animal intelligence.
summary: Gallup's 1970 mirror test marks an animal where only a mirror shows it. Few species pass, often not every individual, and it is a sight test that dogs fail.

cards.headline: A chimp reaches for a red mark on its face that it can see only in a mirror.
cards.body: In 1970, psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr. marked chimpanzees with red dye, then gave them a mirror. The chimps used it to examine the marks on their own bodies. So does that mean they know who's in the mirror? And what about animals that fail?

cards.headline: How the mark test works
cards.body: The test runs in stages. First, the animal gets used to the mirror; many attack their reflection, as if it's a rival. Next, they often make odd movements, as if checking who controls the image. Finally, a colored mark goes where the animal can only see it in the mirror. If it pokes at the mark while watching its reflection, it passes.

cards.fact: Few species pass, and not every individual.
cards.context: Great apes, dolphins, elephants and magpies are on the short list. In 2006, researchers at the Bronx Zoo tested three Asian elephants. Only Happy clearly passed, repeatedly touching a white X painted on one side of her head. An invisible mark on the other side checked that she wasn't just reacting to feel or smell. One elephant out of three is a result, not a verdict on every elephant.

mascot.line: Good science: even the test's inventor stays skeptical of a surprising pass.

cards.headline: A test built for eyes
cards.body: Passing is impressive; failing proves less. Dogs usually fail, but dogs live by smell more than sight. In a 2017 smell version of the test, dogs sniffed their own urine longer when an extra odor had been added to it. And when cleaner wrasse fish scraped at marks in 2019, Gallup himself doubted it: they might just be reacting to what looked like a parasite. The mirror asks one question, in one sense.

title: Play
objective: After this level you can explain why young animals play.
summary: Play costs energy yet young animals do it. Canids bow to invite play and keep it fair. Play-deprived rats grow up anxious, so play seems to train social judgment.

cards.headline: Play looks like a waste of energy. Young animals do it anyway.
cards.body: Play has no obvious immediate purpose. It burns energy, and it's noisy and conspicuous: two play-fighting rats could easily catch a hungry hawk's eye. So why does it exist?

cards.headline: "This is just a game"
cards.body: Play fighting uses bites and body slams that could be mistaken for the real thing, so players signal first. Dogs, wolves and coyotes bow: front legs down, back end up. The bow is used almost only in play and always looks the same. After a bow, even growls and bites draw submission or avoidance only about 15 percent of the time. The bow is a promise.

cards.headline: Playing fair
cards.body: Players also hold back. A stronger coyote may not bite as hard as it can, and a dominant animal may roll onto its back to let a weaker partner win for a while. Young rats with the upper hand often give it up the same way. A game where one side always wins stops being a game.

mascot.line: So recess is brain training. I always suspected.

cards.fact: Rats that never play grow up anxious.
cards.context: The old idea was that play is practice for fighting. But play fighting often skips the real moves: young elk lock horns in play, yet never butt heads, which is saved for serious fights. Young rats kept from play fighting grow up anxious, overreact to other rats, and later handle courtship poorly. Researchers think play trains the brain to adjust behavior to the situation.

cards.fact: A fake can beat the real thing.
cards.context: Lorenz found that many instinctive acts are set off only by specific key stimuli. Tinbergen tested which features of a gull's bill trigger a chick's begging pecks, using dummies and varying shape, colors and contrasts. Exaggerate the right features and you get a supernormal stimulus: a fake that draws a stronger response than the real parent. That's why Level 71's chick aims at the red spot: the spot is the key, not the whole parent. The chick isn't recognizing Mom. It's answering a few key signals.

title: Darwin's Voyage
objective: After this level you can describe what Darwin saw on the voyage of the Beagle.
summary: Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836. He dug up giant sloths related to living ones and saw Galápagos mockingbirds differ by island. The Origin followed in 1859.

cards.headline: In 1831, a 22-year-old boarded HMS Beagle for a five-year trip.
cards.body: Charles Darwin sailed as a companion to the ship's captain, Robert FitzRoy. He came back in 1836 with plants, animals, fossils and notebooks full of field notes. Hidden in that luggage were the clues to one of the biggest ideas in biology. What did he see?

cards.headline: Giant sloths in the ground
cards.body: In Argentina, Darwin dug fossil skulls, thighbones and armor plates out of the ground. Among them were giant ground sloths such as Megatherium, which weighed up to four tonnes. Yet this extinct giant was related to the sloths alive today. Why would the dead giants of a place be family of its living animals?

mascot.line: Every scientist has a box of unlabeled samples. Darwin's just became the most famous one.

cards.fact: Darwin labeled his mockingbirds by island. His finches, not so much.
cards.context: The Beagle reached the Galápagos Islands in September 1835. Darwin noticed the mockingbirds differed on four islands, so he tagged each one with its island. His other birds, which he took for wrens, finches and 'gross-beaks', went home without island labels. Neighboring islands, different mockingbirds: that detail would matter.

cards.headline: The verdict from London
cards.body: Back in England, the bird expert John Gould sorted the specimens. In 1837 he reported that the mockingbirds were three species, each unique to different islands, and that Darwin's mixed bag of wrens, finches and 'gross-beaks' were all ground finches. Neighbors, but not the same species. Darwin began asking how they had diverged from ancestors that arrived from the mainland. His answer came out in 1859: On the Origin of Species.

title: Natural Selection
objective: After this level you can explain how natural selection works.
summary: Natural selection needs variation, differential reproduction and heredity. The Grants saw a 1977 drought favor big-beaked finches, whose young inherited bigger beaks.

cards.headline: Two biologists planned a two-year finch study. It ran for 40.
cards.body: In 1973, Peter and Rosemary Grant began catching and measuring Darwin's finches on Daphne Major in the Galápagos. They expected a short project. Instead, a drought gave them a front-row seat to the idea Darwin's voyage started. First, the idea.

cards.headline: Three ingredients, no chef
cards.body: The National Academies define natural selection as organisms with helpful variations leaving more offspring than others. It needs three ingredients. Variation: some beetles are green, some brown. Differential reproduction: birds eat more green beetles, so brown ones leave more young. Heredity: the young inherit their parents' color. Repeat for generations and brown takes over. Nobody plans it. The birds just keep eating.

mascot.line: Same island, same birds, different menu. The beak that fits the food wins.

cards.fact: In 1977, only 24 millimeters of rain fell on Daphne Major.
cards.context: The small seeds ran out. Medium ground finches, whose short beaks suit small seeds, faced a menu of big, hard ones, and most of the island's finches died. The survivors were the medium ground finches with larger beaks, strong enough to crack the larger seeds. Variation and unequal survival, in one dry year.

cards.headline: The next generation
cards.body: Now the third ingredient. Beak size is inherited, so the survivors' young had measurably larger beaks. The population had changed in about two years. Then the heavy rains of 1982-83 brought plentiful small seeds, smaller-beaked finches fed better, and the average beak slid back down. Selection doesn't aim for bigger. It follows the food.

title: Fossils
objective: After this level you can explain how fossils form and what they show.
summary: Fossils are rare; quick burial lets minerals turn bone to stone, so around 99% are sea animals. Lower rock layers are older, and dated ash layers give ages.

cards.headline: Most living things vanish without a trace when they die.
cards.body: They rot away completely. Yet Darwin could still pull a giant sloth out of the ground. So what does it take for a body to turn to stone, and how can a stack of rock tell you when it lived?

cards.headline: How bone becomes stone
cards.body: The usual route is petrification. An animal dies and its soft parts rot, often leaving only bones and teeth, like the vertebrae of Level 3's backbone. Mud, sand or silt buries them before they vanish. More layers pile on and press down until they become sedimentary rock, while water seeping through leaves minerals in the bones, turning them to stone. It takes thousands or even millions of years. Slow cooking, extreme edition.

mascot.line: Somewhere in a museum drawer, very old poo is being handled with great respect.

cards.fact: Around 99% of the fossils we find are from sea animals.
cards.context: Shellfish and sharks lived where sand or mud could bury them quickly, and quick burial is the whole trick. Not every fossil is a body part, either. Bones, teeth and shells are body fossils. Footprints, skin impressions and fossil dung are trace fossils. Yes, fossil dung has a name: coprolites.

cards.headline: Reading the layers
cards.body: Rock builds up like laundry in a hamper: the newest lands on top. So in undisturbed layers, lower fossils are older than higher ones, a rule called superposition. For real dates, geologists measure radioactive elements, which decay at known rates, in volcanic ash above and below a fossil. That's how one set of trilobites was pinned between 520 and 545 million years old. Compare layers worldwide and you get the geologic timescale.

cards.headline: One supercontinent, then many

After a mass extinction at the end of the Triassic, the dinosaurs survived and spread into new forms. Then Pangaea broke apart. Dinosaurs ended up on separate continents and evolved independently, like cousins raised in different countries. The result: more and more kinds of dinosaur.

cards.context: Plentiful Jurassic plants fed plant-eaters like Diplodocus and Brachiosaurus, and in the Cretaceous the titanosaurs grew bigger still. title: Birds Are Dinosaurs
objective: After this level you can explain the evidence that birds descend from dinosaurs.
summary: Birds evolved from small theropod dinosaurs. Archaeopteryx mixed feathers with teeth and a bony tail; Sinosauropteryx had feathers. Birds outlived the other dinosaurs.

cards.headline: The pigeon on your windowsill is a dinosaur.
cards.body: Not dinosaur-ish. A dinosaur, from the same group of meat-eaters as Tyrannosaurus rex. It sounds like a joke until you see the fossils. So what's the evidence?

cards.fact: Archaeopteryx had feathers, teeth and a long bony tail.
cards.context: Its fossils, about 150 million years old, turned up in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany starting in 1861, two years after Darwin's Origin. It had feathered wings like a bird, but also well-developed teeth, three clawed fingers and a long bony tail like smaller dinosaurs. Its skeleton shares many features with a group of theropods. Part bird, part dinosaur, right on the line.

mascot.line: Picture a fluffy little dinosaur. Now you've pictured it correctly.

cards.headline: Feathers came first
cards.body: In 1996, a fossil hunter in China found Sinosauropteryx, a small meat-eating theropod covered in thin, hair-like feathers. It wasn't directly related to birds. It was the first feathered dinosaur discovered outside the bird line. So feathers weren't a bird invention at all. They were already on dinosaurs.

cards.headline: The dinosaurs that made it
cards.body: Birds evolved from small theropods, the meat-eating group that includes T. rex. The oldest bird-like fossils, over 150 million years old, still had sharp teeth; beaks came later. When the end-Cretaceous extinction struck 66 million years ago, every other dinosaur died out. Birds didn't. So the birds on Level 1's list of five vertebrate groups are living dinosaurs too. You've probably heard one this morning.

cards.headline: The clue in the clay
cards.body: In 1980, physicist Luis Alvarez and his geologist son Walter studied a thin layer of clay found around the world at the end of the Cretaceous. It was rich in iridium, a metal rare on Earth but more abundant in meteorites. Their idea: a huge asteroid impact. It was controversial at first. Then there's the crater, Chicxulub, centred on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula and the same age as the extinction. Today it's the most widely accepted explanation.

cards.fact: The asteroid was about 10 to 15 km wide.

Volcanic eruptions in India were already stressing life, but the asteroid was the final blow.

title: From Water to Land
objective: After this level you can explain how fish-like animals first came onto land.
summary: Tiktaalik, a 375-million-year-old fish, had gills and scales plus a neck and wrist-like fin bones. It was found in rocks of the age its finders predicted.

cards.headline: Every time you bend your wrist, thank a fish.
cards.body: So says Neil Shubin, and he means a real fish that lived in streams 375 million years ago. He helped find it, and his team knew roughly where to look before they started digging.

cards.headline: They predicted where to dig
cards.body: Earlier research suggested the move onto land happened about 375 million years ago, in rivers. So the team hunted in 375-million-year-old rocks that had preserved a river delta. In 2004, on Ellesmere Island in Arctic Canada, a team led by Neil Shubin, Edward Daeschler and Farish Jenkins found it: Tiktaalik. The National Academy of Sciences cites it as a prediction of evolutionary theory confirmed. Not dig and hope. Dig where the theory points.

cards.headline: A fish that did push-ups
cards.body: Tiktaalik was still a fish. But its sturdy fin bones let it prop itself up in shallow water, and its neck let it turn its head while its body rested on the bottom. Its shoulder, elbow and wrist use the same bones as your upper arm, forearm and wrist. It sits on the path to the four-legged vertebrates: amphibians, dinosaurs, birds and mammals, you included.

title: Peppered Moths
objective: After this level you can explain the peppered moth as evolution people could watch.
summary: Dark peppered moths spread as soot hid them from birds, then declined as the air cleaned. Majerus's experiment, published in 2012, confirmed bird predation.

cards.headline: In 1848, a black peppered moth turned up in Manchester.
cards.body: Peppered moths were normally light-colored. By 1898, dark moths there outnumbered light ones 99 to 1. That's evolution fast enough to watch from a city window. What happened?

cards.headline: Soot changes the hiding game
cards.body: Peppered moths rest on tree bark by day, and birds hunt them there. Then the Industrial Revolution coated trees in coal soot and killed the pale lichens. A light moth on black bark stood out; a dark one blended in. Birds ate more light moths and fewer dark ones, and the dark form took over. It's Level 82's beetles again, with wings.

cards.headline: Then the air cleaned up
cards.body: Once the soot eased, the story ran in reverse: since about 1970, dark peppered moths in Britain have rapidly become rarer. But some scientists attacked the classic experiments and doubted that birds were really the cause. Someone had to test it properly.

mascot.line: Six years of moth-watching, finished by friends. Science can be a team sport.

cards.fact: Michael Majerus released 4,864 moths to settle the question.
cards.context: Over six years near Cambridge, the largest experiment of its kind, he let moths settle naturally at low density and watched the birds. Birds took dark moths more often than pale ones, enough to explain their decline. Majerus died in 2009 before publishing, so colleagues analysed his data and published it in 2012: the most direct evidence yet for camouflage and bird predation.

The National Academy of Sciences says there is no scientific controversy about its basic facts: it has survived testing by many thousands of scientists for more than a century.

title: Domestication
objective: After this level you can explain how people tamed dogs, cattle and horses.
summary: Taming changes one animal; domestication changes a line over generations. All cattle trace to about 80 aurochs; modern horses to the Volga-Don steppe around 2200 BCE.

cards.headline: Every farmed cow on Earth descends from about 80 wild animals.
cards.body: They were aurochs, wild oxen, and they were no pushovers: just keeping them captive was hard work. So how does a wild animal become a farm animal, and what did people change along the way?

cards.headline: Tame is not the same as domesticated
cards.body: A tamed animal is one individual that has learned to put up with people. Its heredity hasn't changed. Domestication goes deeper: over many generations, people choose which animals breed, and choosing calm, docile animals has been central to it. The changes pass from parent to young. Dogs came first, domesticated by hunter-gatherers before anyone farmed. Taming takes one lifetime. Domestication takes many.

mascot.line: Eighty ancestors for every cow alive. That's one very crowded family tree.

cards.fact: All domestic cattle trace back to a small herd of aurochs.
cards.context: DNA from ancient cattle bones dug up in Iran points to about 80 aurochs, domesticated in the Near East about 10,500 years ago. Their wild relatives didn't last. The aurochs survived in central Poland until 1627, then vanished. The wild ox is gone; its farmyard descendants are the line that stayed.

cards.headline: Horses: bred for calm and a strong back
cards.body: Ancient DNA from 273 horses shows where today's domestic horses began: the western Eurasian steppes, especially the lower Volga-Don region, around 2200 BCE. From there they spread across Eurasia and replaced other horses. Two genetic changes stand out in them: one linked to more docile behavior, one pointing to a stronger backbone. People weren't just catching horses. They were breeding better ones to ride.

title: Endangered Species
objective: After this level you can explain why species become endangered.
summary: The IUCN Red List ranks species from Least Concern to Extinct; three rungs count as threatened. In 2025, 47,187 of 169,420 evaluated species were. Habitat loss leads.

cards.headline: 47,187 species are officially threatened with extinction.
cards.body: That's the count in the IUCN Red List, version 2025-1, from March 2025: the world's main scorecard for species at risk. What do its labels mean, and why do species end up on it?

cards.headline: A ladder from safe to gone
cards.body: The Red List puts each assessed species on one rung of a ladder: Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, Extinct. Three middle rungs, Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered, together count as threatened. Two extra labels sit off the ladder: Data Deficient (not enough is known) and Not Evaluated. Threatened isn't one label. It's three rungs of the same ladder.

cards.fact: About 41 percent of amphibian species are threatened.
cards.context: That's IUCN's best estimate in version 2025-1, against about 27 percent of mammals. Across all 169,420 species evaluated, 47,187 are threatened. Remember Level 2's 1.5 million named animals, a million of them insects? Only about 1 percent of described insect species have been evaluated at all. The list is a partial census, not a full one.

mascot.line: One rung up is real progress. It's also a reminder of how many rungs are left.

cards.headline: Why species slide down the ladder
cards.body: The most pervasive threat is habitat loss: land cleared for farms, logging and building. Introduced species, climate change, pollution, overhunting and disease pile on. Level 6's giant panda shows both sides. Logging and clearing broke its forest into patches, isolating small groups, and as few as 1,864 live wild. Yet in 2016 IUCN moved it from Endangered to Vulnerable. One rung up, still on the ladder.

title: Gone in Our Time

cards.headline: The last passenger pigeon had a name: Martha.
cards.body: She died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914, and her species died with her. She wasn't the first animal lost in modern times, or the last. Here are three, and in every one, people played the leading part.

cards.fact: The dodo was a flightless relative of pigeons.
cards.context: It lived only on Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean. When sailors arrived, they hunted it, and the animals they brought ashore, pigs, dogs, cats and rats, preyed on it too. A bird that couldn't fly, on an island it couldn't leave, had nowhere to go. It was gone by the late 1600s.

mascot.line: A huge number is not the same as a safe number.

cards.headline: From billions to one
cards.body: When Europeans arrived in North America, there were an estimated 3 to 5 billion passenger pigeons, and migrating flocks darkened the sky for days. People slaughtered them by the millions each year and shipped them by the railway carload to city markets. Martha outlived them all. When she died in 1914, her body was frozen in a block of ice and sent to the Smithsonian.

title: Saving Species
objective: After this level you can describe conservation successes, like the bald eagle.
summary: DDT left 417 bald eagle pairs in 1963; after the 1972 ban they recovered. Condors bred in captivity now number over 500. Humpbacks rebounded after whaling stopped.

cards.headline: By 1987, every wild California condor had been caught on purpose.
cards.body: North America's largest land bird, with a 9.5-foot wingspan, was down so far that all the remaining wild ones went into a captive breeding program. A last resort. Did it work? And what saved the bald eagle and the humpback whale?

cards.headline: The eagle and the eggshell
cards.body: The pesticide DDT washed into rivers and lakes, where water plants and fish absorbed it. Bald eagles ate the fish and took in the poison too. It made their eggshells so thin that eggs often broke during incubation. By 1963, only 417 nesting pairs were known in the lower 48 states. The poison didn't have to kill the adults. It just had to stop the next generation.

mascot.line: From 417 pairs to more than 71,000. That's a comeback worth saluting.

cards.fact: Bald eagles: from 417 nesting pairs to about 316,700 birds.
cards.context: The US banned DDT in 1972, and the eagles rebuilt. In 2007, the bald eagle came off the list of threatened and endangered species. A USFWS estimate from 2018 and 2019 surveys counts about 316,700 bald eagles in the lower 48 states, including 71,467 breeding pairs. Remove the poison, and the eagles did the rest.

cards.headline: Condors and humpbacks
cards.body: Captive-bred condors have been going back to the wild since 1992, and the total population is now more than 500. Their top known killer is lead, from ammunition fragments scavenging condors swallow. Humpback whales needed something simpler: people had to stop hunting them. Whaling had cut most populations by more than 95 percent before a final moratorium in 1985. In 2016, NOAA found 9 of 14 humpback populations no longer needed listing.

title: Invasive Species
objective: After this level you can explain how animals brought to new places can harm them.
summary: An invasive species harms a place where it isn't native. Cane toads missed Queensland's beetles and spread; brown treesnakes helped wipe out 9 of Guam's 11 forest birds.

cards.headline: In 1935, Australia imported toads to eat beetles. The beetles barely noticed.
cards.body: Queensland's sugarcane farmers had a beetle problem, so cane toads were released to eat them. The toads thrived; the beetles carried on. Today cane toads number in the millions. So when does a newcomer become a problem?

cards.headline: In the wrong place, doing harm
cards.body: An invasive species is one that causes ecological or economic harm in a place where it isn't native. Most get there with people's help, on purpose or by accident. Once there, they can compete with native animals for food and space, change habitats and even drive native species extinct. Being new isn't the problem. Doing damage is.

mascot.line: Hired to fix one problem, became a much bigger one. We've all had a week like that.

cards.fact: Cane toads now number in the millions in Australia.
cards.context: In 1935, 2,400 were released on Queensland sugarcane farms to control beetles. They had little or no effect on the beetles, but they spread across northeastern Australia, and they're still moving west about 40 to 60 km a year. Their poison kills many native predators that try to eat them. The pest control became the pest.

cards.headline: A stowaway on Guam
cards.body: The brown treesnake is native to places such as New Guinea and Australia. During or soon after World War II, it reached Guam hidden in cargo. There it helped wipe out 9 of the island's 11 native forest bird species. It even climbs power lines and causes expensive outages. Guam's forests lost most of their native birds to one hitchhiker.

title: Animals in Space
objective: After this level you can describe the animals that flew in space before humans.
summary: Fruit flies went first (1947). Laika was the first creature in orbit (1957) and died within hours. Belka and Strelka came home in 1960; Ham flew in 1961, before Gagarin.

cards.headline: The first animals in space were fruit flies.
cards.body: In 1947 they rode a rocket up and came back alive. Why send animals into space before people, and what did it cost them?

cards.headline: Could a body survive up there?
cards.body: Nobody knew what spaceflight would do to a living body. One big worry was that people might not survive long periods of weightlessness. Radiation was another unknown. So on 20 February 1947, fruit flies went up on a V-2 rocket; they were small, light and easy to store. Back on the ground, scientists found no radiation-caused changes to their genetics. The tiniest passengers cleared the way.

cards.fact: Laika was the first living creature to orbit Earth.
cards.context: She was a stray from the streets of Moscow, launched on Sputnik 2 on November 3, 1957. The spacecraft had no way to bring her home, and she died from overheating about five to seven hours into the flight. For years, Soviet officials said she had lived for days; the truth came out in 2002. Today a statue honors her in Moscow.

title: Ideas From Animals
objective: After this level you can name inventions inspired by animals, like Velcro.
summary: Biomimicry copies nature's designs: Velcro from burdock burrs, a Shinkansen nose from a kingfisher's beak, and NASA grippers from gecko toe hairs.

cards.headline: Velcro began as burrs stuck in a dog's fur.
cards.body: Burrs come from burdock, a plant, not an animal. But the idea behind Velcro, copying designs that living things already use, has a name: biomimicry. And animals have handed engineers some brilliant designs.

cards.headline: Hooks meet loops
cards.body: Near Lausanne, Switzerland, George de Mestral came home from a walk with burdock burrs stuck to his clothes and his dog's fur. Under a microscope, each burr was covered in tiny hooks. He paired hooks with fabric loops and patented the fastener in 1955. The name blends two French words: velours, velvet, and crochet, hook. Nature drew the plans; he did the sewing.

mascot.line: Diving into water, entering a tunnel: same problem, same solution.

cards.fact: A bird's beak quieted a bullet train.
cards.context: Early Shinkansen trains made a loud 'tunnel boom' as they left tunnels, disturbing people nearby. Engineers turned to the kingfisher, whose long, pointed beak lets it dive into water with barely a splash. JR West's 500 Series, in service from 1997, got a nose shaped like that beak. The booms stopped, and the train ran faster on less electricity.

cards.headline: Sticky without glue
cards.body: Geckos are small reptiles that climb smooth walls on toe pads covered in tiny hairs, the smallest hundreds of times thinner than a human hair. They stick by van der Waals forces: weak, temporary attractions between atoms. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory copied the trick with synthetic hairs that grip when pressed and let go when the force is removed. They even work in a vacuum, handy for grabbing things in space.
